person/jim-chanos.text:
Jim Chanos is one of Wall Street's best-known short sellers, and pretty much the prototype of the accounting-forensic kind. He founded Kynikos Associates in 1985 as a hedge fund built around short selling, made his name flagging Baldwin-United in the 1980s, shorted Enron ahead of its 2001 collapse, and later warned on Tyco, China's economy, and dot-com-era telecom names. He closed client funds in 2023 and converted Kynikos to a family office, but he never stopped teaching — a Yale graduate, he has long been an adjunct professor at the Yale School of Management and the University of Wisconsin-Madison — or commenting on fraud and market excess. In recent years his target has been AI-driven semiconductor and data-center valuations, which is exactly where this corpus catches up with him.

Our coverage comes from a single appearance: a June 20, 2026 interview on The Monetary Matters Network. The thesis on display is classic Chanos — less "AI is a bubble" than "the accounting doesn't add up." His central claim is "a significant timing disconnect wherein chip suppliers recognize revenues immediately while hyperscalers capitalize their massive infrastructure cost" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)) — the picks-and-shovels sellers "are recognizing revenues and profits immediately" while the spending side spreads the bill over years ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). That leads him to hunt for what he calls "inherently unprofitable business models that are attached to this AI ecosystem," and to dismiss the demand forecasts underpinning capex: "I really take a jaundiced eye on these forecasts of just immense need for compute at today's prices" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

The specific calls are pointed. He is deeply skeptical of "neo-cloud" data-center developers like CoreWeave, modeling a very generous ten-year GPU depreciation lifespan and still finding the economics wanting ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). On Tesla, at nearly a two-trillion-dollar valuation, he argues "you have to believe in Mars and the moon and data centers in space to justify almost two trillion dollars," tying the story to promises "built on a rocket that has not yet achieved Earth orbit... and has blown up" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). His macro frame is deliberately deflating: US growth was "virtually the same in the decade before the introduction of the internet versus after," and in the fiber-optic cycle S&P operating profits rose roughly 30% over two years into the earnings peak — then dropped 40% ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

The interesting wrinkle is that the file's lone bullish tag belongs to Nvidia. Chanos jokes with clients that you want to be long the chip producers, "not where the chips reside," and concedes the multiples have compressed — "Nvidia's at like 15 times on 2027 EPS," while "Broadcom, after the decline this morning, is at 12 times 2028 EPS" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). He frames it as "a market in which there's going to be opportunities on both the long and the short side," and offers the kicker: "if you really want to be scared, I'll tell you that I'm net long AI versus my short" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

A caveat on the record: everything above dates from that one interview, so no evolution of his views is observable here — the heavily bearish stance mix (20 bearish tags against 7 neutral and 1 bullish, several of them resting on the same quotes) reflects a single conversation's tilt rather than a tracked arc. What it does capture is the shape of Chanos's argument: he is not betting against the technology, he is betting that the accounting eventually forces the unprofitable parts of the AI ecosystem to show their hand.

ticker/GC=F.text:
The gold debate in this corpus is less a fight over direction than a standoff over two price levels: $4,100 on the downside and $4,400 on the top. By mid-June 2026 the metal had been through a meaningful selloff — a guest analyst noted on June 17 that "gold sold off pretty significantly" — and was grinding sideways in the low $4,300s, with [Patrick Ceresna](../People/patrick-ceresna.md) clocking a 4.5% push to 4,321 and an unattributed host describing gold as "steady sideways, holding its value." The headline consensus reads bullish (8 bullish vs. 5 bearish), but with 29 neutral calls the honest characterization is that most watchers were waiting to see which level broke first.

The bear case rests almost entirely on [Jeffrey Christian](../People/jeffrey-christian.md), who was consistent and specific across June 19 and 23: he expects the $4,100 level to be tested ("we do expect that level to be tested"), and if it gives way, a technical target of around $3,800 — or $3,500 on a short-term spike. He's scenario-mapping more than pounding the table, but the digest tags all four of his calls as down. The only other outright bearish note came from that same June 17 guest analyst, and by August an unidentified commentator was openly skeptical of the "$8,000" chatter — arguing that what looked like a pause was "more likely to bend first, then decline" — even while conceding that if prices keep running, "gold continues to get a bid." That's a hedge, not a thesis.

The bull side is louder. [Erik Townsend](../People/erik-townsend.md) called gold "set to rally spectacularly" once the Iran oil dislocation and its knock-on inflation effects work through, and he and [Patrick Ceresna](../People/patrick-ceresna.md) both saw the bounce extending to the $4,400 area, where a declining 50-day moving average sits just overhead. [George Noble](../People/george-noble.md) framed $4,200 gold as part of a broader "down with fiat currency" trade. The June 17 host told listeners to "upsize your gold position here and or buy gold miners," targeting "45 and change" before resistance bites, with the 200-day around 4,400-ish. Most interesting is [Jeffrey Kushin](../People/jeffrey-kushin.md), who anchored his bullishness in CPM Group's 2014 call to buy at $1,211 — "we were a few years early" — while simultaneously relaying CPM's own view that $4,100 would be tested again over the next two and a half months. In other words, even the bull was channeling Christian's levels.

The timeline itself is compressed and a little ragged: nearly everything clusters in a single week (June 16–23, 2026), with Christian's bearish notes and Noble's bullish one landing the same day, and then a two-month gap to the unattributed August 13 commentary about $8,000. There are same-day contradictions worth flagging — the June 17 host was tagged both flat and up within one session, and Ceresna's stance wobbled between unspecified and up on June 18. Coverage is also thin in places: the August quotes carry no attribution, one entry is blank, and several quotes are truncated mid-sentence. What the record does show clearly is a market staring at $4,100 versus $4,400 with conviction concentrated in a handful of named voices — Christian on one side, Townsend, Noble and Kushin on the other — and everyone else on the fence.

theme/rates-bonds.text:
The corpus for Rates, Bonds & the Dollar is substantial in volume — 27 tickered calls and 107 broad views — but unusually thin in attribution: every entry arrives stripped of speaker names and citation links, so the "key voices" here can only be identified by date and position rather than by name. The tickers themselves tell you where the attention is: the 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX, 13 calls) and the dollar index (DX-Y.NYB, 9), with the yen pairs trailing behind. On rates, the corpus is remarkably unambiguous. On August 3 one participant stated flatly that "I think bond yields are going to move higher," and by August 11 that had hardened into "bond markets suffering. In other words, yields going up." Nobody in the extracted material makes the case for lower yields; the bond market is treated as the pressure point everyone is watching.

The dollar is where the debate turns genuinely combative, and it whipsaws inside a single week. On August 3 the technical read was bearish: "the dollar is breaking an uptrend. We just fell through some support levels right at the 100 101 level." Three days later, on August 6, the same instrument produced the opposite conclusion — "the long-term moving average for the dollar is saying hey it is going up. It has all the characteristics of a bull market." Whether that's two analysts disagreeing or one analyst capitulating and flipping is impossible to tell without names, which is frustrating, because it's the most interesting question in the tape. The yen commentary has the same problem in mirror image: an August 6 call that "the yen would continue going down because the fundamentals point to going down" sits against an August 3 warning that a "strengthening of the yen in yields moving higher should collapse that yen carry trade." The corpus holds both the yen-grinds-lower and the yen-snaps-higher scenarios simultaneously, and the August 7 framing explains why it matters: "if the yen were to weaken substantially, then the other currencies would follow it," because "a stable yen is not only important for the US, but it's very important for the entire region."

Underneath the fast-moving chart talk sits a slower, more structural argument that got louder as the period progressed. On August 11 one voice argued that "the reserve asset dimension of the dollar is definitely going to decline. I think we could see the dollar down to as little as 40…" — a genuinely extreme endpoint, whatever index it's measured against. The same day produced the counterintuitive companion view that "the dollar is very strong, unusually strong. Our currency should be a lot weaker than it is given our fiscal situation." These two are not really opponents; both are dollar-skeptics, one forecasting reserve-driven collapse and the other complaining the currency is still overvalued given US fiscal math. The July 25 material adds the plumbing behind that unease: "India's demand for dollars has repeatedly exceeded the private supply available at prevailing exchange rates," post-2008 bank constraints have pushed dollar funding into swaps, and regional currency interventions have reliably produced "a temporary rally followed by renewed depreciation." Notably, the corpus never reconciles that offshore dollar scarcity with calls for the index at 40 — the shortage story and the collapse story coexist without a referee.

The tone shift across the window is the clearest pattern of all. Late July is structural and monetary-plumbing in register — funding markets, intervention failure rates, balance sheet constraints. August is faster and more tactical: support levels, moving averages, carry-trade triggers, and even a hint of official-sector involvement in the August 7 fragment "Treasury Takes Control Of Volatility." The constants through both registers are rising yields and a dollar whose problems are framed as cumulative rather than cyclical. What the digest cannot support is any verdict on who has been right — with no names, no links, and a cluster of entries (August 11 and July 28 among them) whose quotes extracted as blank, this page can map the shape of the argument but not score the arguers.

person/ash-bennington.text:
Ash Bennington is an American financial journalist and editor whose career tracks the evolution of financial media itself: more than a decade at Bloomberg News as an economics editor directing coverage of the U.S. and global economy, followed by a move to Real Vision, where he became managing editor and one of the platform's most prominent on-air personalities. There he hosts daily markets programming — including the show "Catalysts" — and conducts long-form interviews with investors, economists, central-bank watchers, and digital-asset leaders. His signature is macro-focused commentary that works the seam between traditional finance and crypto, treating them as one contiguous story rather than two camps, which is a posture well suited to Real Vision's audience and a reason he shows up so often as a guest and moderator across finance podcasts and conferences.

The record available for this page, however, is thin, and it is worth saying so plainly. The digest logs Bennington as an interview guest on two occasions but carries no dated stances — no bullish or bearish calls, no position shifts, no quotes to anchor a timeline — so there is nothing here to chart how his views may have moved over time. That absence fits his actual role in these conversations: he is closer to moderator than advocate, drawing out guests' convictions rather than staking aggressive calls of his own. Until transcripts surface with specific, dated positions, this page can describe the venue and the posture, not a portfolio of predictions.

person/brent-johnson.text:
Brent Johnson is an American investor and macro commentator who spent roughly a decade as a financial advisor at Credit Suisse before striking out on his own to found Santiago Capital, a boutique firm built around capital preservation and gold ownership. He is best known in macro circles for his Dollar Milkshake Theory, a framework he popularized through relentless podcast appearances across the 2010s and 2020s — to the point where the theory, and Johnson himself, became fixtures of the fin-media circuit. He is also a longtime, outspoken advocate of gold as a store of value, which makes his recent commentary all the more interesting.

The Milkshake thesis, in Johnson's own telling, was never simply "strong dollar" cheerleading — "part of the milkshake initially was saying interest rates would rise and treasury bonds would fall" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). The core conviction is that the dollar's dominance ends, if it ends, through strength rather than collapse: "if the dollar is ever going to die, it's going to die of strength and it's not going to die because it got inflated away and went to zero" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). By mid-2026 he had folded stablecoins into this story, calling them "a revolution that many just don't yet understand" and noting that "99% of all outstanding stable coins in the world today are US dollar stable coins" — digital demand for dollars, in effect ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). His geopolitical analog is blunt: "more likely we see the fall of the republic and the rise of the empire than the fall of the empire and some new power takeover" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)).

His June 2026 appearance on MacroVoices (#537) shows him at his most concrete. On oil, he expects the market to "go fill those gaps at least up to 85" and says "I wouldn't be surprised if we're back over 100 before the year is out" — while framing his earlier "$150 to $200 by year end" view against what he calls the "doomsday prediction" school ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). On the just-signed Iran deal he is flatly skeptical: "I think this is a very very tenuous deal at best. And as I said at the very beginning, I don't expect it to last," with more wars and less cooperation "probably in our future" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). He also flagged that "National defense is I think probably going to be the biggest investment opportunity any of us have ever seen," warned of a "potential food cascade later this year or next year" via disrupted fertilizer and crop-input supply chains, and noted that historically "75% of the time" when markets moved outside a certain band, "sovereigns around the world went into distress" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). Most striking for a gold advocate: he conceded that "from the moment the war broke out in Iran to the moment that it looked like we were getting this deal signed last week, gold fell 20%" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)).

The corpus on Johnson is thin — two guest entries, both pointing to the same MacroVoices episode — so the day-over-day "stance flips" logged between June 18 and June 19, 2026 should be read as one interview catalogued twice, not a genuine pivot. His overall stance mix (18 bullish / 16 bearish / 23 neutral) fits the man: a dollar bull and gold owner who hedges nearly every call, and whose strongest conviction is less about any single asset than about volatility itself — fluid situations, tenuous deals, and knock-on effects arriving "three to six months" later.

person/cpm-group-analyst.text:
The corpus knows this figure only as an analyst at CPM Group, the precious metals research consultancy, and their footprint here is a single appearance: a June 16, 2026 guest spot on a gold and silver market update. Even from that one sit-down, though, a clear posture emerges. This is a bull on the precious metals complex — gold, silver, platinum and palladium — and one whose bullion case leans heavily on CPM's own institutional track record rather than on macro hand-waving. The headline claim is a performance stat: "If I bought and sold and shorted gold when CPM Group said buy gold, sell gold. Then I have a 14.3% an annual annualized rate of return" ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). That is a strong, checkable boast — the analyst is effectively asking the audience to trust the firm's timing signals because following them, on their telling, would have compounded money at double digits.

The analytical style on display is historical analogy. "We were saying, 'Hey, this thing's looking scarily like the late 1980s,'" the analyst recalled of an earlier call ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)) — an invocation of a period that precious metals veterans read as a long, grinding aftermath to a prior bull cycle, which makes the bullish framing of that remark notable; the digest tags it as a bullish stance, but the analogy itself cuts both ways depending on which part of the 1980s parallel one emphasizes. The fundamental case underneath is more measured than the bravado suggests: on physical supply and demand, the analyst allowed that markets "got pretty tight, but we did not have deficits... more skewed to the upside" ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)) — tightness without outright shortage, with the balance of risk tilted toward higher prices.

That is the honest limit of the portrait. One appearance, one date, three data points, all bullish-to-neutral on the same complex. There is no bearish call anywhere in the record, and no timeline across which to trace a shift in view — whether this analyst ever turned cautious on gold, or whether the 14.3% claim survives scrutiny in weaker stretches, is simply not documented here. What the digest does establish is a personality type: a firm-loyalist bull who argues from CPM's own signal history and from rhymes with the 1980s, and who hedges the physical picture even while skewing the outlook upward.

person/cpm-group-speaker.text:
The "CPM Group speaker" is, as the byline suggests, an unidentified representative of CPM Group — the New York precious metals research and consultancy house — rather than a named analyst, and the corpus holds exactly one appearance from them: a June 23, 2026 spot on the CPM Group channel framed as a warning that new risks were building fast in gold and silver markets ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)). That single interview is the entire record here, so this portrait is a snapshot rather than a track record.

What the speaker argues is a fairly classic hard-money construction: the case for bullion is built on a pessimistic read of the credit system. On the bearish side of the ledger, they contend that the "United States is half of what it was 25 years ago," and they flag structural rot in lending itself — "loans that are disguised so that they're not loans so that they don't have to show up on balance sheets" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)). The direction of travel is clear: a shrinking American economic footprint plus opaque, off-balance-sheet credit is exactly the mix that erodes confidence in paper claims.

The tell is that this credit pessimism isn't the conclusion — it's the premise. The speaker lands squarely bullish on precious metals, closing the loop with "And that all put together is good for gold and silver" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)). In other words, the bearish credit call and the bullish metals call are the same trade viewed from two angles. With only one dated appearance and no prior or subsequent statements in the record, there is nothing to establish how these views have moved over time; readers should treat this as a single, internally consistent data point from the CPM Group camp.

person/chris-semenuk.text:
Chris Semenuk is a U.S. portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price who came up as an industrials equity analyst covering machinery and electrical-equipment companies, and his one sustained public appearance reads exactly like that pedigree. On June 18, 2026, in an interview on The Monetary Matters Network, he argued that the boom in electricity demand from AI data centers is best bought through the industrial and equipment supply chain — gas-turbine and switchgear makers, electrical gear, and grid/services names such as Caterpillar, Timken, Quanta Services, Powell Industries, Eaton, GE Vernova, and Cognex — rather than through merchant utilities like Talen, Vistra, and Constellation, which he noted have at times traded at "Nvidia-type" multiples ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). In a debate that has mostly been framed as utilities-versus-chips, Semenuk's contribution is insisting the real expression sits in the equipment layer between them.

The macro scaffolding for that call is a cycle claim: US manufacturing "has essentially been in a recession for three straight years and we have only just emerged now," with the ISM PMI survey only recently getting back to roughly 50, and reindustrialization "still in its very early stages" ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). From there he works down the chain: "the single largest investment opportunities will be in equipment. So, any type of equipment that is used to make stuff," and his favorite flavor is the deliberately unglamorous one — "boring" short-cycle companies making ball bearings, pneumatics, and filters, which he thinks "are poised to actually overearn because they have cost bases which they've worked on over the last few years" ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)).

The specific calls are unusually concrete. On Caterpillar, he cites a backlog "north of $60 billion" and argues the company is "capable of at least $10 a quarter by 2029" — implying earnings power roughly double the ~$20 a share of today — while lumping Cat in with peers he calls "extraordinarily well-managed businesses that have enormous cash flow" ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). On Eaton, he points to "240% growth in equipment that they sell into data centers" last quarter and the elegant fact that "they make everything from the grid straight down to the chip inside the data center" ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). On GE Vernova his line is quotable and self-aware — "The next Vernova is Vernova" — with the kicker that the most underappreciated part of the business isn't the $87 billion backlog but an $80 billion piece he thinks the market is missing; Timken gets the robotics-adjacent angle (actuators, and "all the parts that go into those humanoids"), and Cognex stands in for machine vision ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). His bearish side is aimed at the hottest part of the AI-power trade: "behind the meter is nonsense," and AI is only 6–7% of US electricity consumption versus manufacturing's 26% — a reminder that the grid story predates the data-center frenzy ([The Longest US Manufacturing Recession in History is Finall…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aS6W2GJ2AzA)). He is also candid about the base rates he's fighting, conceding these industrial stocks "have generally been licenses to lose money," even if industrial-construction demand has lately changed that.

The caveat is that this is a one-interview record. Everything cited here comes from that single June 2026 appearance, so the heavily bullish stance mix (48 bullish tags against 13 bearish and 11 neutral) reflects one sitting rather than a track record, and there is no timeline yet showing how Semenuk's views move when the cycle does. What exists is a coherent snapshot: an equipment specialist betting that the least glamorous corner of the market is where the power-and-reindustrialization theme pays.

person/david-woo.text:
David Woo is a macro strategist cut from the old Wall Street cloth: a decade at Bank of America Merrill Lynch as managing director and head of global rates, currencies and emerging-markets research, preceded by a stint at Barclays, and a reputation built on outspoken, contrarian calls — he was among the first sell-side voices to publish valuation work on bitcoin, and has long weighed in on currency wars, oil and geopolitics. He left the sell side around 2019 to go independent, and now publishes the newsletter and interview series "David Woo Unbound" while making the podcast rounds as a macro commenter. In this corpus he appears once, on The Monetary Matters Network, and the record skews heavily negative: 22 bearish stances against 13 bullish and 2 neutral.

That single appearance, on June 15, 2026, captures Woo at his most contrarian. His headline call is a short on the Nasdaq — "I'm short. I mean, I've been short for a while, so it's been very painful" — and the framing is distinctly his: "my big issue with the whole entire AI thing is that AI has gotten too good for his own good," by which he means the technology is now good enough to threaten the economics of the very companies promoting it, inviting a regulatory and corporate backlash ([Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It's Simply Too Good) | Dav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)). His supporting evidence is concrete: the combined capex of the five hyperscalers was "down for the first time in three years" on a quarter-on-quarter comparison, Microsoft canceled most of its Claude Code licenses to push employees onto GitHub Copilot, and the Nasdaq's $5 trillion market-cap addition has been driven, in his telling, mainly by retail buyers — a crowd he suspects was shaken by the "bearish key reversal week" he flagged. He also expects second-quarter earnings deceleration and warns that a recession would hit advertising-dependent AI winners hard ([Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It's Simply Too Good) | Dav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)).

The bullish side of the ledger is oil, and it is a geopolitical trade. With the Iran-Israel conflict jeopardizing the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, Woo is "heavily bullish" on crude and has put a number on it: $150 a barrel if the strait is still closed by the end of July ([Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It's Simply Too Good) | Dav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)). He says the trade has already paid — "thank God I made some money... from being long oil, so I haven't done so badly this year" — and he treats the Middle East endgame with a trader's indifference to the path: whatever the outcome, he cares only that oil stays bid. The rest of the portfolio is one coordinated macro stance, in his own words "bullish oil and bearish equities and... bearish gold," with the gold view explicitly short-term and unambiguous in his mind ([Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It's Simply Too Good) | Dav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)).

What the record here cannot show is movement. Every stance in the corpus is dated to that one June 2026 conversation, so there is no before-and-after to trace; his admission that the Nasdaq short has been on "for a while" and has "been very painful" hints at positions predating the coverage, but the archive offers no earlier marker to anchor them ([Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It's Simply Too Good) | Dav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)). For now, the portrait is a snapshot: a former bank economist betting against the AI trade and for war-priced oil — a classic Woo posture, but one documented here on a single day.

person/ed-zitron.text:
Ed Zitron is an American writer who has become one of the loudest and most quotable critics of the modern technology industry. He cut his teeth as a technology and video-game journalist before crossing over into public relations, where he founded the firm EZ-PR, and he now runs the newsletter "Where's Your Ed At" — the venue where he coined the term "Rot Economy" for a style of management obsessed with growth and metrics at the direct expense of products and users. His 2024 essay "The Man Who Killed Google Search," which laid Google's search decline at the feet of managerial dysfunction rather than technological necessity, was widely circulated, and since 2024 he has hosted the podcast "Better Offline." In market terms, he is a one-note bear in the best sense of the phrase: his entire analytical project is the argument that generative AI is a capital-incinerating bubble, and he repeats it with unusual specificity.

His core case, laid out in his June 21, 2026 appearance on The Monetary Matters Network, is that "the sheer size of the losses by the large language model (LLM) companies are unsustainable" and that the operational costs of training and running these models dwarf anything the technology actually earns ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). His framing is a daisy chain of red ink: "Every AI company's unprofitable. The largest customers of AI compute are unprofitable. Their customers also unprofitable" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). After "trillion plus dollars" spent, he argues, "the fact we're still debating the ROI kind of says everything" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)).

His hardest call in the corpus is a dated one: asked whether the AI bubble pops in 2027 or 2028, he answered "I think 2027's the safe bet" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). He backs the timing with a supply-demand argument — the compute demand "does not exist," the heavy spenders are unprofitable AI companies, and the industry would need "two or three more OpenAI and Anthropic sized customers that do not exist" plus "hundreds of billions of dollars" of AI compute revenue to justify the buildout ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). He is openly skeptical of the Broadcom–OpenAI announcement, made the previous October, of 10 gigawatts of AI data centers ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)), and he reads the coming financing wave — roughly "$150 billion within the next 6 to 12 months," much of it via IPOs — not as AI demand but as "a demand for speculative debt" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). Even Nvidia, whose revenue he ties to this spending, gets only a countdown: "two, three more earnings calls" if guidance stops making markets "rock hard" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)). The moral edge of his argument is aimed at who pays: he says the industry is trying to "dump these companies on retail investors who are going to be the victims of this theological hype cycle" ([Ed Zitron: The AI Bubble is Bleeding Cash, Here Are The Rec…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc)).

A caveat on the record: this corpus captures only that single June 2026 appearance, with 32 bearish stances, three neutral, and not one bullish — so there is no observed evolution in his views here, only consistency. The neutral tags on Microsoft and Nvidia look like artifacts of how the quotes were classified rather than genuine hedging; nothing in the transcript suggests he sees a bull case anywhere in the chain.

person/emmanuel-macron.text:
Emmanuel Macron is a French politician who has served as President of France since 2017, winning re-election in 2022 after first defeating Marine Le Pen, but his route to the Élysée ran through finance. After training as an Inspecteur des finances in the French civil service, he joined Rothschild & Cie Banque in 2008 and made partner as a dealmaker; the deal that defined his banking career was advising Nestlé on its roughly $12 billion acquisition of Pfizer's infant-nutrition business in 2012, which reportedly earned him a large bonus and the press nickname "the Mozart of finance." He left banking for politics in 2012, serving as deputy secretary-general of the Élysée Palace (2012–2014) and then Minister of Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs (2014–2016) under François Hollande, before founding the centrist En Marche! movement — now Renaissance — and taking the presidency in 2017. That background matters for how one reads his market commentary: this is a head of state who genuinely understands deal structures and capital markets, not a politician improvising on topics beyond his depth.

On markets, the record logged here is thin but pointed. As of June 20, 2026, Macron was bearish on the concentration of value in US technology, warning that if the United States could "turn off the switch" from one day to the next, it would damage the multi-trillion-dollar companies leading the AI sector ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)). The taggers filed this single statement under two headings — AI & Semiconductors and Rates, Bonds & the Dollar — which reads less like two separate calls and more like one argument about American financial and technological dominance: that the US position is powerful precisely because it is centralized, and therefore fragile. It is essentially a sovereignty-and-dependency critique dressed in market language, the kind of warning you would expect from a French president who spent his banking career watching cross-border deals depend on a handful of jurisdictions.

Honesty requires flagging the limits of this file. The stance log shows two bearish entries and nothing bullish or neutral, but both entries trace back to the same June 2026 statement and the same source, so the true sample is one dated call, not two. There is no earlier baseline in the digest against which to measure a shift — no pre-2026 view on AI, chips, or the dollar — so it is impossible to say whether June 2026 marked a turn in his thinking or simply the first time his views were captured here. What can be said is that when Macron did go on the record in this corpus, he went against the consensus story of durable US mega-cap dominance, and he did it with the specificity of someone who knows exactly what a broken deal does to a valuation.

person/eric.text:
This entry is thin. The corpus shows only that a guest identified as Eric has appeared twice on Macro Voices, but the digest contains no extracted stances, dated calls, quotes, or topic timelines for him — no bullish or bearish positions, no chronological shifts, nothing to anchor a portrait of his views. The stance mix is empty across the board, and no citation links were provided to support even those bare appearances.

As it stands, there is not enough verified material to characterize what Eric argues for or how his positioning may have evolved. person/erik-townsend.text:
Erik Townsend is the host of MacroVoices, the weekly macro podcast he built after a career as a software entrepreneur, and the format matters for reading his record: he books big-name guests for long interviews, then uses the companion "Trade of the Week" segment to put his own positioning on tape. The stance log in this corpus skews constructive — 21 bullish calls against 13 bearish and 3 neutral — but that headline tilt undersells how deliberately two-sided his market view is. A caveat is warranted up front: everything documented here comes from a single week of broadcasting in mid-June 2026, centered on episode #537 with Brent Johnson ("There's No Turning Back") and its Trade of the Week companion ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). It is a narrow slice for a portrait of views "over time," but it caught Townsend mid-dislocation, opining on nearly everything that moved.

His signature call that week was oil, and it ran in two directions at once. He was blunt about the flush already underway: "someday we're going to get a real peace deal and when we do, oil is going to sell off and sell off hard. Well, that's exactly what's happened" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). But his forward view was firmly bullish on the supply hole the Iran conflict left behind — "you can't drain 20% of the world's oil reserves and suddenly think that we're going back down to a sustained under 70 level on oil" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). On WTI he flagged a "great big glaring gap in the chart" up to roughly $84.50 and said he expected "prices settle back above 80 at some point here and maybe even as high as 90," while conceding he "wouldn't be surprised if we go lower still as the market continues to celebrate what it thinks is a certain and clean resolution to the Iran deal" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). In the Trade of the Week segment he went further: "I think we're going to go fill those gaps at least up to 85. I wouldn't be surprised if we're back over 100 before the year is out" ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)).

The stance tracker logs oil flipping from bullish to bearish between June 18 and June 19, but that reads less like a change of heart than an artifact of the same episode appearing under multiple upload dates — with bearish quotes about the realized selloff and bullish quotes about the rebound sitting side by side. What's genuinely consistent is his skepticism of the market's euphoria: he noted "the market seems to be celebrating its perception of the Hormuz resolution being unconditionally good for financial markets. I'm a little bit skeptical" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)), and warned that "physical shortages, and the realization that this military conflict might not really be over after all, could all lead to higher prices" ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). The debate he's picking, in short, is with anyone pricing a clean peace.

The rest of the book followed the same war-premium logic. He was bearish the dollar — "The Iran conflict was a source of a lot of that US dollar strength, so a downside retracement makes perfect sense here" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)) — with "a lot more downside as we retrace a lot of the war premium" and the Dixie "back down to 99 and a half... testing what was previously resistance as support" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). Gold he called "set to rally spectacularly after the Iran oil dislocation and associated knock-on inflation effects are really and truly over," though he saw the current bounce capped around the 4,400 level with "a declining 50-day moving average just above" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). Uranium rounded it out: "I remain uber duper bullish long long-term on uranium," with late August to early September as when the market might "catch a bid again" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). The through-line is a macro commentator who fades the consensus celebration, respects the supply shock underneath it, and staggers his bullishness in time rather than holding it all at once.

person/erik-voorhees.text:
Erik Voorhees is an American cryptocurrency entrepreneur and one of Bitcoin's earliest adopters, in the industry since roughly 2011 with a stint at BitInstant in its first chapter. He built the bitcoin betting site SatoshiDice and sold it in 2013, co-founded Coinapult, and is best known for launching the digital asset exchange ShapeShift in 2014, which he ran as CEO through its 2021 decentralization into a DAO before stepping away from day-to-day leadership; more recently he co-founded the privacy-focused AI platform Venice AI. The through-line is ideological: a committed libertarian who argues for the "separation of money and state," he tends to reason about markets as a monetary theorist with a portfolio rather than as a chart-watcher.

His corpus presence, it should be said up front, is thin — a single appearance on Raoul Pal's *The Journey Man* (June 18, 2026), in an episode framed around AI, Bitcoin and self-sovereignty. Within that one conversation, though, his strongest call is unambiguous: Bitcoin is "the best form of money that humans have ever created," and in his framing mass adoption follows from that premise almost as a matter of course ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). The conviction extends to the DeFi stack — "the DeFi innovations, lending markets... those tokens deserve to thrive more than they are" — and on whether they will, his answer was flatly "They should and will, but they haven't yet" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). Notably, his explanation for the memecoin era is structural rather than moralistic: the industry "went through this period where everyone was just creating memecoins," he argues, because securities regulation made designing serious tokens too legally dangerous — a "damaging effect of securities regulation" in his telling ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)).

On AI he is tagged neutral, but the substance is pointed. He believes "if I was a frontier lab, I would be very terrified of the open source stuff," noting that "two years ago, it was, you know, comfortably behind the cutting edge" — with the implication that the gap has since closed ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). He also frames the compute race through energy, observing that "China's capacity and ability to produce increasing amounts of energy dwarfs the United States," a line the corpus cross-tags to both China equities and oil & energy ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). His single bearish flag sits in macro and politics, and it is a gloomy one: "you will, I think, see the masses vote for politicians that promise them very damaging things to society," starting — the quote cuts off mid-word — with "stealing from those who pr…" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). That pessimism ties back to his fear of a "stratification of society... sort of like wealth disparity but more like capability disparity," which he raises as an AI-era risk ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)).

The shape of the record, then: three bullish stances (all crypto), one bearish (and political rather than valuation-based), and seven neutral observations, all from one sitting. There is no timeline across which to track his views moving — readers should treat this page as a snapshot of where Voorhees stood in mid-2026, not a record of how he got there.

person/george-gammon.text:
George Gammon is an American real estate investor turned macroeconomic commentator, best known as the creator and host of The Rebel Capitalist Show, a popular YouTube channel and podcast. He cut his teeth fixing and flipping houses before pivoting to the plumbing of the global financial system — the repo market, the Eurodollar system, FX swaps, the Fed's balance sheet, and the role of the US dollar — which he unpacks in trademark whiteboard-style explainers that lean heavily on frameworks popularized by Jeff Snider, a frequent collaborator. A recurring guest on MacroVoices and Real Vision, Gammon has built his brand on skepticism toward official Fed and Treasury narratives, with a standing thesis that the global dollar system is far more fragile than the mainstream admits.

That worldview comes through in his June 20, 2026 video on interest rates, where he dismissed the idea that the central bank is actually in the driver's seat: "Do they really control the interest rate? No, not in my view, just like I didn't control the weather" ([You Won't Believe What Just Happened To Interest Rates (New…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QKGzMIhuh0)). The episode was a reaction piece to a move that "caught the market way offsides, especially the bond market," and Gammon's read ran against the hawkish grain — his strongest call in the record is that investors should "expect lower rates in the future, not higher rates" ([You Won't Believe What Just Happened To Interest Rates (New…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QKGzMIhuh0)). Crucially, he framed falling yields not as a win for borrowers but as a symptom, telling viewers they "have to realize what lower rates tells us about the overall economy" — which, in his reading, usually means the economy is getting weaker, not stronger ([You Won't Believe What Just Happened To Interest Rates (New…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QKGzMIhuh0)).

As evidence, he pointed to plumbing-level signals rather than Fed press conferences, flagging a spread he called "really the key" sitting "right around 30 basis points, which relatively speaking is very low," against a historical norm closer to 100 ([You Won't Believe What Just Happened To Interest Rates (New…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QKGzMIhuh0)). On the policy path itself, he sketched a zigzag — going "from a dove to a hawk and then straight back to a dove again, which would make a lot of sense" — a framing that fits his broader argument that the Fed reacts to forces it doesn't control ([You Won't Believe What Just Happened To Interest Rates (New…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QKGzMIhuh0)).

The honest caveat is that the extracted record here is thin: a single episode from June 2026, with a stance mix of zero bullish, four bearish, and five neutral. That is directionally consistent with Gammon's dollar-fragility thesis — both his rates-and-dollar track and his broad-macro track end flagged bearish on the strength of that one video — but it is far too little to chart how his views have moved over time. What it does capture is the characteristic Gammon posture: read the plumbing, distrust the narrative, and treat falling rates as a recession signal rather than a policy victory.

person/george-noble.text:
George Noble is a Boston-based hedge fund manager and deep-value investor who has run GKO Investment Management since the 1990s, capping a career in the business that stretches back roughly four decades. His shop runs a classic long/short book: patient value longs paired with concentrated, deliberately provocative shorts in richly valued "story" stocks — a list that has publicly included Tesla, Freshpet, SSR Mining and, at one point, Goldman Sachs. The through-line of his public commentary is a bearish macro view on U.S. equities and an open contempt for passive investing, which he treats as the mechanism that keeps money-losing narratives inflated long after fundamentals would justify them.

That worldview comes through plainly in his June 18, 2026 appearance, where he argued that "we are living in a world where reality doesn't matter to the markets whatsoever...the only thing that matters to markets is narrative" ([SpaceX, Iran, OpenAI IPO...Here's My Controversial Stock St…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxR6yvf8ueU)). On the S&P 500 he was blunt both times out: first that "there is absolutely no way that I would go outright long the S&P 500 right now as we speak" ([SpaceX, Iran, OpenAI IPO...Here's My Controversial Stock St…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxR6yvf8ueU)), then five days later that "the S&P relatively speaking is not of interest to me" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). He expects the AI froth to get worse before it breaks — pointing to coming Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs pushing the market "from Mania" into something hotter ([SpaceX, Iran, OpenAI IPO...Here's My Controversial Stock St…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxR6yvf8ueU)) — and he is unusually candid about wanting the reckoning: "Let's say the market falls out of bed, which I think it should do. I actually want it to" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)).

His strongest bullish calls are in hard assets. On oil, he argued on June 18 that "demand for oil is very inelastic," that "there ain't nothing left in the SPR," and that "you could see within the next couple months oil at 150, 170, who knows, maybe even 200" ([SpaceX, Iran, OpenAI IPO...Here's My Controversial Stock St…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxR6yvf8ueU)) — a call he reaffirmed on June 23: "if I had to make a bet on the next 10 or even $15 in crude oil, I would bet higher" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). On gold he is maximalist, noting the dollar fell 9% the prior year while gold rose "60 some odd percent," and declaring "I have a dream that one day gold will be at $8,000, $10,000, $12,000" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). His fiat skepticism stops short of crypto: "Bitcoin is the Facebook of speculative assets... I think it's just going to go into the sunset" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)).

The record on how his views move is thin — two interviews, on George Gammon's show and The Macro Dirt Podcast, five days apart in June 2026 — so there is little genuine timeline to trace. The one flagged stance change, a June 18 bearish to June 23 bullish flip on rates and the dollar, looks more like labeling noise than a real reversal: his "bullish" June 23 quote is about fiat being "a waste of time," and in the same conversation he said of the dollar "I actually think it goes lower if you must know," consistent with a man who is structurally short the buck and long gold ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). Treat his positioning as a coherent, standing macro view — narrative-driven equities down, oil and gold up, Bitcoin irrelevant — awaiting a longer record to confirm or break it.

person/grant-williams.text:
Grant Williams is a veteran financial markets commentator and newsletter author who spent roughly three decades in finance, the bulk of it trading and analyzing bond and credit markets across Asia — stints in Tokyo, Singapore, Sydney and Hong Kong — before relocating to the United States. That credit-market pedigree matters to how he frames things: he came up in the plumbing of the financial system rather than on an equity sales desk, and it shows in a worldview that treats macroeconomics, monetary policy and financial history as the real drivers of markets. He is best known as the author and publisher of the contrarian macro newsletter "Things That Make You Go Hmmm...," a vehicle that cemented his reputation for skeptical, big-picture commentary on markets and central-bank policy.

His larger public profile, though, was built on media. In 2014 he co-founded the financial media platform Real Vision with Raoul Pal, and there he created and hosted interview series such as "The End Game" — long-form conversations that became a staple for investors who wanted depth over soundbites. After leaving Real Vision in 2022, he set up his own venture centered on "The Grant Williams Podcast," continuing the same format: extended interviews with investors, economists and historians, with gold and monetary policy as recurring themes. He remains a frequent speaker and podcast guest on macro and financial history.

A caveat on the record here: this corpus contains only a single appearance by Williams — as a guest on Maggie Lake's Talking Markets — and the extraction captured no directional calls, bullish or bearish, on any topic. So while his public identity is plainly contrarian and central-bank-skeptical, there are no dated, citable stances in this dataset to trace how his views may have moved over time. Anyone looking for his strongest specific calls will need a richer intake of his podcast appearances and newsletter output than what is currently logged.

person/grok.text:
Grok is the rare "person" in this corpus who isn't one at all: it is the AI chatbot built by xAI, the artificial-intelligence company Elon Musk founded, first released in November 2023 and since iterated through Grok-1 up to Grok-2, Grok-3 and Grok-4, distinguishable by real-time access to data from X (formerly Twitter) and a deliberately irreverent, humorous persona. Its single credited appearance here — a solo slot on Hong Kong economist 徐家健's show — almost certainly refers to the chatbot itself being conversed with or quizzed on air rather than to a human market guest. That framing matters for everything below: commentary filed under Grok's name is machine-generated synthesis, not the conviction of an investor with money on the line.

The one entry on its timeline is a neutral-marked take on China and Hong Kong equities dated June 28, 2026, centred on JD.com's crowd-swamping entry into Hong Kong retail — the Wan Chai mall opening that drew long queues and packed foot traffic from day one. Grok's diagnosis is that the "迫爆" spectacle carries unmistakable traits of involution (內卷): JD is committing more than 350億 of investment into a saturated market already under "retail apocalypse" pressure — high rents, weak consumption, spending drained northward across the border — and pairing its supply-chain muscle with aggressive promotions (half-price offers, daily 20%-off deals) to accelerate a price war that deepens the survival crisis for incumbents like Fortress (豐澤), ParknShop (百佳) and HKTVmall ([零售末日 京東迫爆](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48974)). It is a vivid, descriptive read on competitive dynamics but noncommittal on trade implications, which is presumably why the entry is tagged neutral rather than a bullish or bearish call on the sector.

The coverage here is thin, and should be stated plainly: one observation, zero bullish calls, zero bearish calls, and no discernible movement in views over time. Treat this page as a snapshot of a single sharp, machine-written vignette on Hong Kong's retail price war rather than a track record. If further Grok segments surface, the interesting question will be whether the bot's stances remain summaries of the human debate around it — as this one largely is — or whether anyone ought to score an AI's output like a pundit's calls at all.

person/grok-xai.text:
Grok is an oddity in this corpus because it is not a person at all. It is the AI chatbot built by xAI, the artificial intelligence company Elon Musk founded in 2023, positioned as a real-time, irreverent rival to ChatGPT and wired into the X platform. It has no fund, no track record, and no career in markets — yet it has begun appearing on podcasts and media programs as a "guest," with hosts reading out or featuring its AI-generated analysis. Its sole entry here comes from exactly that setup: a featured appearance on the Chinese-language economics and finance podcast of Hong Kong economist 徐家健 (Eric Tsang Ka-kin), offering commentary on hot IPOs.

That single appearance, dated June 16, 2026, produced its only logged call — a studiedly neutral one on SpaceX. While the surrounding commentary ran hot (the hosting article frames the debate around a Nobel laureate blasting SpaceX as a Ponzi scheme), Grok split the difference. It cautioned that historically, large first-day "pop" IPOs in heated markets tend to show weak three-year post-adjustment returns, weighed down by profit-taking, lockup-expiry selling pressure, and mean reversion, and argued investors should treat the listing as high-volatility growth exposure whose outcome hinges on Starlink profitability and Starship execution rather than first-day enthusiasm ([SpaceX市值一飛沖天 諾獎得主狠批龐氏騙局](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)). The framing is textbook risk-factor language — closer to a synthesized literature review than a positioned call, which is arguably the honest way to describe what a chatbot's "view" is.

The record here is thin and should be read as such: one appearance, one topic, one neutral stance, with zero bullish or bearish entries, so there is no timeline along which its views could be said to have moved. Whether an AI's outputs belong in an analyst corpus at all is a fair question the data cannot answer; for now, Grok's profile amounts to a single, hedged, sensible-sounding IPO warning delivered secondhand through a podcast host.

person/jd.text:
JD is, at least as this corpus records them, a repeat guest of The Macro Dirt Podcast rather than a household name — two appearances a week apart in June 2026 — and the record offers little beyond that: no firm, no title, just a stance ledger running 7 bullish, 6 bearish, and 3 neutral across the two sittings. What the transcripts do establish is a coherent disposition: bearish the dollar and the U.S. equity index, aggressively positioned in bonds, and willing to concentrate nearly all of their optimism in a single outsized name — SpaceX.

The dollar short is the anchor call. On June 17 JD was already there — "I'm still bearish on the dollar... the thesis is the same" — resting on the view that rate cuts are coming and the currency won't survive them, paired with an unambiguous duration preference: "I like bonds. I like the front end of the yield curve. I like the back end of the yield curve... I like the dollar short" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). By June 23 the view had hardened into a false-breakout call — "I'm very bearish" — and the bond stance had escalated from liking to loading: "I'm putting it all in bonds" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). The digest flags the rates/bonds/dollar bucket as flipping bullish to bearish between the two shows, but the substance reads less like a reversal than a sharpening: on June 23 JD spelled out the mechanism — "What I'm betting is that the correlation is going to turn negative. And I think what does that is a sharp decline in stocks like maybe even a crash" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). The trade only pays, in other words, if equities break.

The equity bear case is a concentration story: "the S&P is now 22% semiconductors, all-time high... I'm very bearish on the index" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). Yet the same guest who expects a crash-flavored unwind is maximalist on one name. On June 17: "if there was one stock that could 5x from here in the top 10 of the S&P, it's probably SpaceX," with a scenario where it "goes parabolic, and everything else becomes a funding trade" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). By June 23 the target had been raised: "if there was any stock that had a chance of going to a 10 trillion market cap, it would be SpaceX. And I still believe that" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). The S&P framing is the guest's own — SpaceX is privately held — but that is the claim as recorded, and it is the one position that never wavered.

The rest of the book is quieter: bullish crude ("I'm actually I'm with you guys," deferring to the hosts on oil), and two outright holds — "I'm keeping Brazil" and "I'm keeping energy" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). Worth saying plainly: this is a thin record. Two podcast appearances inside a single week, no biographical detail, and one transcript garbled enough that a policymaker's name comes through as "Worsche." What exists is a snapshot of a positioned macro bear — short dollars, all-in on duration, out of the index, long one rocket company — not a career arc, and how these views move from here is untested by the available data.

person/jack-farley.text:
Jack Farley is an American financial podcaster and interviewer, best known as the host of Forward Guidance, a macro-focused interview show covering monetary policy, credit markets, and digital assets. He launched the program at Blockworks — originally under the Blockworks TV banner — and later carried it forward independently. Before that, he produced and hosted crypto and macro content at Real Vision. A Stanford University graduate, Farley has built his reputation on long-form conversations with macro investors, credit analysts, and crypto market practitioners, and he appears in this corpus three times as an interview guest, affiliated with The Monetary Matters Network.

What the record here does not show is a set of market calls. The digest contains no dated positions — nothing bullish, bearish, or neutral — and no topic timeline tracking how his views may have shifted over time. That absence is unsurprising given his role: Farley's job is to draw out the arguments of his guests rather than to plant his own flag on a trade, and a corpus built from his appearances will naturally capture other people's calls rather than his. The honest portrait, then, is of an interviewer and convener of macro debate rather than a positioned commentator, and any account of his personal market views would need sourcing well beyond what this digest provides.

person/jared-dillian.text:
Jared Dillian is an American finance writer and former Wall Street trader who has built his second career on being the kind of commentator his first career taught him to distrust: plain-spoken, macro-obsessed, and allergic to consensus. He is best known as the publisher of The Daily Dirtnap, a widely read daily commentary letter on macroeconomics, markets, and trading, and as the author of the "10th Man" investment column for Mauldin Economics. Before all that, he spent roughly a decade on Wall Street, most notably on Lehman Brothers' fixed income and ETF trading desk — a seat that put him front row for both the September 11 attacks and the firm's 2008 collapse, and which he chronicled in his 2011 memoir, "Street Freak: Money and Madness at Lehman Brothers." Earlier still, he served as an officer in the U.S. Coast Guard, a resume detail that fits the survivalist streak running through his public persona as a frequent podcast guest and speaker known for contrarian macro takes and essays on money and culture.

The record digested here, however, is thin on the substance of his calls. Dillian appears twice as a guest on The Macro Dirt Podcast, but the extracted facts contain no scored bullish, bearish, or neutral stances and no dated market positions — nothing that would let an honest portrait trace how his views have moved over time or isolate his strongest calls. Given that his entire brand rests on timing and contrarian positioning, that gap matters; for now, this page can establish who Dillian is, but the evidence base for what he has argued, and when, awaits fuller transcript coverage.

person/jeff.text:
"Jeff" is, for now, one of the thinner entries in this corpus: a two-time interview guest on Eurodollar University, tracked by first name only, with both appearances logged in June 2026. That paucity of biography is worth stating plainly up front, because what the record lacks in depth it makes up for in conviction — five bullish tags, two neutral, and not a single bearish call across the two sit-downs.

His strongest call came on oil. Appearing on June 14, 2026 in [Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E), he framed the post-Iran supply picture with the old adage "up like a rocket, down like a feather" — oil prices "scream higher when the supply gets restricted" — and then committed to the near term: "oil prices are not going to go back down to $50 where they're eventually going to go. That's absolutely the case. The question is how long they take…" ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). Read closely, that is really a two-part call — sticky-high prices now, an eventual slide toward $50 later, with the clock the only open variable. Bullish on the way up, patient on the way down.

A week later, on June 21, 2026, his attention had shifted to the global rates complex, and the corpus tags him outright bullish there: "Swiss bond rates are almost back at zero all over again. The critical two-year instrument yielding just a couple of basis points" ([Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4)), and "Chinese rates are similarly ultra and that curve is bull steepening" ([Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4)). The same appearance carries a bullish tag on Chinese equities on the strength of that bull-steepening observation, alongside a more hedged read of curve dynamics — the front end going up while "the long end of the curve was saying, 'Wait a minute. Hold on here… growth and inflation expectations now are cle…'" ([Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4)). The tell is the episode's own title: a "dire warning to the world." His bullishness on bonds is bullish the way a fire alarm is bullish for exits — he is long the flight-to-quality trade because he believes the world's bond markets are pricing a downturn everyone else is ignoring.

As for how his views have moved, there is barely an arc to draw. Within the single June 14 appearance he hedged oil with an even-handed framing before landing on the bullish side of it, and by June 21 he had moved on entirely to the deflationary signal coming out of Switzerland and China. What the timeline does show is a consistent shape to the man's thinking: supply-driven stickiness in crude, collapsing yields and bull-steepening curves abroad as the real story, and zero recorded bearish positions. Whether that reflects a genuinely one-sided book or simply a guest whose two appearances happened to catch him mid-warning, the record so far cannot say.

person/jeff-jeoff.text:
Jeff (listed in some records as "Jeoff") is a macro commentator whose footprint in this corpus rests on a single appearance — a June 14, 2026 guest spot on Eurodollar University, a show closely associated with the bearish, Eurodollar-system school of macro analysis. The profile is thin by design: one interview, one day, one tightly argued thesis. But within that narrow window he stakes out an unambiguous position, with six of his eight tagged statements bearish and none bullish, spanning oil prices, broad macro conditions, and China ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)).

His strongest and most specific call is a downside target on crude. With the Iran risk premium fading, he argues the market's "fundamental value is what we saw in December, not what we had, you know, in the middle of April" — and that the arithmetic of collapsing demand leads ultimately to $50-a-barrel oil ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). The evidence he leans on hardest is Chinese demand destruction: physical crude imports to China were "down by 3% in March, 20% in April, and 29% in May," a deterioration steep enough that he treats it as the defining data point of the cycle ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). Layered on top is a macro argument that cuts against consensus: energy shocks "are not inflationary. They end up destroying demand, especially for an economy that's weak to begin with... They don't end in inflation" — a direct rebuttal to the supply-shock-driven inflation narrative ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)).

What keeps him from being a pure perma-bear on tape is tactical flexibility. He expects front-end oil prices "to come down and then bounce," and tells viewers the first tell will be watching "WTI futures to see how the curve reshapes in this next stage" rather than the spot price itself ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). That is a trader's concession inside a structural bear case — direction down, path choppy. Because the entire record here dates from a single June 2026 interview, there is no basis to trace how his views have evolved; whether the $50 call and the energy-shocks-aren't-inflationary thesis hardened or softened afterward is simply not documented in this corpus.

person/jeff-snider.text:
Jeff Snider is an American macroeconomic researcher and commentator, formerly Head of Global Research and Investment Strategy at Alhambra Investment Partners and now the host of Eurodollar University, the podcast and newsletter he runs with longtime collaborator Emil Kalinowski. He is best known as the leading proponent of the "Eurodollar" framework: the argument that the vast offshore dollar banking system — not central banks or official money printing — is the true global monetary system, and that its contraction since 2008 explains chronic disinflation, sluggish growth, recurring liquidity squeezes, and the limits of Federal Reserve policy. A prolific Real Vision contributor with thousands of commentaries behind him, Snider treats Treasury curves, T-bill spreads, Fed repo operations, and WTI contango/backwardation as real-time gauges of global dollar liquidity, which is why his asset calls are almost always liquidity calls underneath.

The record captured here is concentrated in a ten-day window in mid-June 2026, and it is unrelentingly bearish. His loudest call of the stretch came on June 13, when he branded the ECB's rate hike a historic mistake — "The European Central Bank just raised rates on Thursday into an economy that is already shrinking" ([Europe Just Made A Historic Policy Mistake](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo)). He reached for a 2008 analogy, noting Ben Bernanke had come dangerously close to hiking even after Bear Stearns had already failed while the US economy was weakening, and insisted that "the Treasury market response in 2008 is the key parallel to what's going on today" ([Europe Just Made A Historic Policy Mistake](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo)). The Fed, he warned, "has to decide whether it's going to see through the oil shock or get pulled into the same mistake," even as "there's a private credit bust going on in Europe at the same time, too" ([Europe Just Made A Historic Policy Mistake](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo)). Notably, his stance on rates, bonds and the dollar flipped within days — bullish on the 2008-parallel bond rally on June 13, bearish by June 15, reasoning that if dollar-yen stops tracking rate differentials then something else, presumably liquidity, is driving it.

China is where his bearishness turns apocalyptic. On June 16 he flagged that "Chinese households are not just borrowing less. They are pulling back at a pace we have not seen before in comparable data," and that real estate investment falling 16.2% in the first five months of the year is "not some mild downturn. This is a legit collapse" ([China Confirms The Rumors...Is This The Start Of A Financia…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d7cNjW_mcEM)). He paired that with contracting May retail sales, deflationary signals from China's curves, and the observation that "no amount of stimulus has been able to thaw the deepening freeze and it starts with the banks who are under siege" ([China Confirms The Rumors...Is This The Start Of A Financia…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d7cNjW_mcEM)). By June 20 he had escalated to the big picture: "China's completing its own transition into depression economics with consequences that have and will continue to radiate all over the entire planet," with the Hang Seng "not behaving like a market convinced by the recovery story" ([Something VERY Strange is Happening Just Happened Global Ma…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3j8NhL0FTo4)). He extended the political-economy read to the UK on June 22: "It is the economy, stupid. It is the single biggest lesson from Starmer's fall" ([The U.K. Has Fallen: Here's What It Means for the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wL63-KdtuEE)).

His most distinctive calls, though, are the curve-reading ones. When oil plunged on June 18, he rejected the headline explanation of an Iran peace deal and supply normalization, arguing instead that "oil is falling because demand may already be breaking" — while still expecting a short-run WTI bounce and telling viewers to watch whether the front of the curve flips into contango, "just like we were doing at the end of last year" ([ALERT: Oil And Interest Rates Are PLUNGING, Here's What You…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IpZ_HYxaU_8)). On private credit the same week, he argued the problem has shifted from insiders to "those on the outside who no longer want in," a development he said puts the system "even deeper into stage three" of his framework ([MASSIVE Private Credit Update, Here's What You Must know](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9WH-0Pl9ydM)).

The shape of the ledger is telling: 6 bullish calls against 91 bearish and 17 neutral in the captured sample, with the lone green pocket in AI and semiconductors, where he observed on June 20 that "US stocks are surging, tech is soaring, semiconductors are vertical" — even while hedging that Hong Kong's China-linked money flows may be telling a story the AI trade ignores ([Something VERY Strange is Happening Just Happened Global Ma…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3j8NhL0FTo4)). The coverage here is thin in span — essentially June 13–22, 2026 — so it reads as a snapshot of a persistently bearish posture rather than a long arc. The through-line is the framework itself: in Snider's telling, every one of these calls, from Frankfurt's policy mistake to China's "depression economics" to a demand-driven oil slide, is the post-2008 Eurodollar contraction showing up in a different market.

person/jeffrey-christian.text:
Jeffrey Christian is one of the old hands of precious metals research. He cut his teeth trading and researching the metals desk at J. Aron & Company in the late 1970s before founding CPM Group, the New York commodities research and advisory shop he has run since 1986. CPM's annual Gold and Silver Yearbooks remain standard reference points for supply-and-demand work on gold, silver, platinum, and palladium, and Christian himself has advised miners, fabricators, central banks, and investors, testified before the CFTC on metals market structure and position limits, and cropped up as a steady media commentator. In recent years he has also wandered into digital assets, offering Ethereum price views alongside his traditional metals coverage. He is, in short, a fundamentals man — which makes the tape of calls captured here, overwhelmingly technical in framing, an interesting window onto how he communicates in a fast market.

The record skews distinctly cautious: of the calls extracted across his appearances, 22 register bearish against 10 neutral and just 6 bullish. The center of gravity is gold. On June 19, 2026, with gold holding above $4,000 in what he called a volatile consolidation, Christian was blunt that "prices are subject to be tested again at the 4,100 level. We do expect that level to be tested," and that a break below "is possible probably on a shorter term spike possibly with a target of 3,800 or 3,500" ([Why Gold and Silver Prices Are Falling: Is Now The Time To …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1btQrMgRwo)). By June 23 he had sharpened it: gold was testing $4,100, and "a break below 4,100 would have a technical target of around $3,800" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)).
