Silver followed a similar arc — from a $60–$90 range framing on June 16 ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)), to a June 19 warning that "the potential of a spike below 60 is very high at least for the next two and a half months" before prices strengthen later ([Why Gold and Silver Prices Are Falling: Is Now The Time To …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1btQrMgRwo)), to June 23, when silver was testing the low $60s and he flagged that "there are people with 54 and $50 targets" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)). The platinum group he was simply bearish on throughout: palladium "back down testing that 1,200 support level" with the price at 1,262 after touching 1,245 on June 19, platinum heading lower over the next few months, with $1,500 a level technical traders were watching by June 23.

What keeps this from being a simple bear profile is the explicit time horizon. Christian's downside calls are tactical — spikes, tests, flushes — wrapped inside a structurally constructive view. On June 23 he argued the very risks building in the broader economy "may be negative for the broader economy but supportive for gold and silver over time" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)), the same week he said Fed commentary pointed to continued volatility across financial markets and metals ([Why Gold and Silver Prices Are Falling: Is Now The Time To …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1btQrMgRwo)). He also brings a policy edge, criticizing pressure for the Fed to be "less forthcoming with information, less transparent, more secretive," and dismissing AI as "generating a tremendous amount of misinformation, bad information, inaccurate information" ([Gold And Silver Price WARNING: New Risks Are Building Fast!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o)) — skepticism aimed less at any one asset than at the quality of information moving markets.

The honest caveat is that this record is thin and narrow: three appearances inside a single week of June 2026. What looks like an "evolution" — from neutral consolidation talk on June 16 to explicit $3,800 gold targets and sub-$60 silver warnings by June 23 — may be nothing more than a market confirmng his levels in real time. Whether this near-term bearishness reflects his standing posture or a moment-in-time call, the corpus here cannot say; his four decades of Yearbook-style supply-and-demand work suggests the framework is the constant, and the targets are the weather.

person/jeffrey-kushin.text:
Jeffrey Kushin is a consultant and market analyst at CPM Group, the New York-based commodities research and consulting firm founded by Jeffrey Christian that has made precious metals its specialty. He works across the firm's research, consulting, and commentary on gold, silver, platinum, and palladium, and fronts CPM's video outlooks, where he translates the firm's supply-demand modeling into price forecasts ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Coverage here is thin — a single appearance in this corpus — so the portrait rests almost entirely on one outing.

That outing, a June 16, 2026 market update, shows a analyst who argues in ranges and time windows rather than slogans. On gold, he called for a "volatile sideways consolidation between now and September" with roughly $4,000 on the low end ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)), and said CPM expected the $4,100 level to be tested again over the following two and a half months, adding that "it may well hold" with further support at $3,800 and below ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Silver got the same structure but a more constructive ending: a "very wide range" of $60 to $90 for the next two and a half to three months, "and then higher prices in the final four months of this year" ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)).

The interesting part of the video is the split within precious metals. Platinum he treated bearishly, expecting a $1,600 to $2,000 trade over the next couple of months with a downside skew "because there's greater bearishness" in that market ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)), and palladium likewise as trading sideways "with a downward bend" as bullishness that emerged the prior June continued to bleed out ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Underneath the near-term chop, though, his framework is unabashedly fundamentalist: he leaned on CPM's long record, noting that when gold fell to $1,211 in 2014, "we said buy. We were a few years early," with the price having risen since on the firm's supply-demand analysis ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). The candor about being early is telling — this is a shop that would rather be directionally right on fundamentals than tactically punctual.

Because everything on record comes from this one appearance, there is no observable evolution in Kushin's views — the bullish and bearish tags reflect different metals within a single outlook, not a shift over time. Whether he bends more hawkish or dovish on gold as the September window he flagged approaches is, for now, unanswered.

person/jim-zelter.text:
Jim Zelter is one of the most powerful figures in American credit markets, and his résumé explains why. He cut his teeth at Citigroup in high-yield sales and trading and proprietary trading before joining Apollo Global Management in 2006, where he built the firm's capital markets business and helped turn Apollo into a credit powerhouse. He was elevated to Co-President in 2018 alongside Scott Kleinman, and in early 2025 he became sole President of Apollo and joined its board — a move widely read as positioning him as a potential successor to CEO Marc Rowan. He holds an undergraduate degree from Duke and an MBA from Wharton. In short, when Zelter talks about credit, he is speaking about a market he has spent two decades shaping from the inside.

For all that standing, his footprint in this corpus is thin: a single guest appearance on Eurodollar University, and no bullish or bearish calls on record — only one neutral stance. On the topic of credit, private credit and BDCs, his logged comment came on June 23, 2026, when he struck a measured tone on private credit default rates, allowing for "maybe even a little bit of an increase" ([Private Credit Default Rates Just Hit The Point Of No Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SibAV9HRe1I)) — a notably muted take on a debate that often skews apocalyptic. With one appearance and one data point, there is no observable arc in his views yet; this page should be revisited if he surfaces again.

person/joseph.text:
Joseph Wang is the markets commentator known across macro-finance circles as "Fed Guy," a moniker earned the hard way: he spent years as a senior trader on the Markets Desk — the Open Market Trading Desk at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — where he helped execute the Fed's Treasury and quantitative easing operations. That insider pedigree is the spine of his public work. He wrote *Central Banking 101* in 2021, runs the Fed Guy blog and newsletter on Fed policy, reserves, liquidity, and money markets, and now splits his time between appearing as a podcast guest and hosting his own show. When Wang talks about plumbing — reserves, repo, the desk's mechanics — he's speaking with unusual authority; when he ranges into trade and geopolitics, he's a macro tourist like the rest of us, and the record below shows both modes.

The captured record here is thin and narrow — essentially one week in June 2026 — so it is a snapshot rather than a trajectory, and no honest claim about how his views have "moved over time" can be made from it. What the snapshot shows is a decidedly bearish tilt: eleven bearish stances against three bullish and four neutral across the tracked items. His strongest call is blunt. On his June 2026 FOMC Debrief he said the pieces "all point to me to a sustained and meaningful decline in risk assets" ([June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)) — no hedging there. Around it, on Markets Weekly dated June 20, 2026, he flagged the collapse in crude — "if you look at spot oil prices, they've absolutely plummeted... you can see spot Brent all the way down" — and read it as "a large, large disinflationary wave" ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)). For a rates-desk veteran, leading with the disinflation channel rather than the geopolitical one is telling.

The same episode sketches his geopolitical frame, and it is more mixed than the risk-asset call. He argued the post-Iran-war "ceasefire that is probably going to hold" and speculated the conflict might mark "the twilight of the influence" of the region's hardliners — a constructive read ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)). On trade he is gloomier and more animated: he sees "the Chinese moving up the value chain and threatening a wider range of industries in the West," notes that Beijing manages the currency so that it is "structurally undervalued," and observes that Germany's export decline has been a big drag on its growth — with "Euroland" now weighing its own tariff wall in response ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)). The one place he stays deliberately neutral is rates itself: despite the disinflation impulse, he simply observes that markets are "still pricing in an ongoing mini rate hiking cycle" ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)).

So the portrait that survives this record is of a former desk trader turned public commentator whose June 2026 posture was bearish on risk assets, oil, and the Western trade position, grudgingly impressed by China's industrial ascent, and noncommittal on the rate path. Whether that is a durable worldview or one week's reading of the tape, the corpus as it stands cannot say — more appearances, especially from earlier periods, would be needed before calling him a perma-bear.

person/joseph-wang.text:
Joseph Wang is a financial markets commentator best known as "Fed Guy," the name attached to his newsletter and research platform FedGuy.com, which concentrates on Federal Reserve policy, market liquidity, and the plumbing of the financial system. His credibility on those topics comes from the inside: he was previously a senior trader on the Open Markets Desk at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, executing monetary policy through trades in Treasuries, agency MBS, and repo. He is also the author of *Central Banking 101* (2021) and has served as chief investment officer at Monetary Macro, a macro-focused investment firm, while building a steady presence as a podcast guest on Fed operations, quantitative easing, money markets, and dollar liquidity.

That background shapes the way he argues. Wang is not primarily a calls-on-the-tape macro pundit; his lens is operational — how the Fed's balance sheet, the repo market, and liquidity mechanics translate policy into asset prices. When he does take market stances, they tend to come bundled with a view of what the Fed is mechanically likely to do, and in the single appearance captured here that combination is on full display.

The documented record is thin — one interview, the [June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI) — so there is no observable evolution in his views across time, only a snapshot. In that snapshot his rates call was firmly neutral: "No, I don't think we'll hike this year. ... my base case is that we just hold rates throughout this year" ([June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)). Around that hold-rates baseline sit two positions the record tags as bearish. On energy, he was explicit: "energy prices are coming down. Uh they're going to come down maybe rapidly, and so that is going to have a disinflationary tailwind coming forward" ([June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)). And on the rates complex, he argued that the Fed achieved tightening without moving: "he didn't have to actually hike. He did tighten financial conditions and raise rates just by his communication" ([June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)).

Those three pieces are not in tension so much as a coherent package: no formal hikes expected, falling energy as a disinflationary tailwind, and policy effectively tighter anyway because of hawkish rhetoric. The overall stance mix — zero bullish, two bearish, two neutral — is consistent with a commentator more comfortable describing the machinery than pounding the table. A fuller portrait of how Wang's views move across a cycle will require more appearances than this corpus currently holds.

person/maggie-lake.text:
Maggie Lake is a financial journalist and media entrepreneur rather than a market caller, and that distinction shapes everything about how she shows up in this corpus. She spent roughly two decades at CNN as a business anchor and correspondent in New York, covering global markets, the economy, and corporate news, and hosting programs including "Marketplace Africa." She left CNN in 2022 and moved into independent financial media, launching the "Maggie Lake: Talking Markets" newsletter and podcast, where she interviews investors, economists, and market practitioners about macroeconomics and investing. She has also been associated with Real Vision as a host and interviewer, and her signature is accessible, jargon-free breakdowns of macro and market themes aimed at a general audience rather than at specialists.

On the record collected here, she appears exactly once, as an interview guest, and carries no classified market stances at all — zero bullish, zero bearish, zero neutral — with no dated calls or position shifts to trace. That is not a hedge or an evasion on her part; it reflects her actual role in the debate. Lake is a translator and convener, the person who gets practitioners to explain their views clearly, not someone staking her own directional claims on gold, equities, or rates. Readers looking for her strongest calls with dates will not find them in this corpus, and the honest portrait is that her contribution runs through the quality of the conversations she hosts rather than through positions she has taken. The timeline section, in short, is thin by nature of the subject, not by neglect.

person/max-sweaty.text:
Max Sweaty is a figure of thin record in this corpus: he appears exactly once, as an interview guest on The Monetary Matters Network, and that single appearance is the full extent of his documented footprint here. No transcript excerpts, quotes, or named positions were extracted from the conversation, so what he argued for on that show — if he argued for anything at all — is not preserved in the source material underpinning this page.

The classification record is likewise empty: no bullish, bearish, or neutral stances were assigned to him across any topic, and there is no topic timeline to speak of. As a result, this page cannot chart any evolution in his views, name any signature calls, or place him within a broader debate. Readers should treat the absence of detail here as a statement about coverage, not a statement about the person; building out a substantive portrait of Max Sweaty would require either a fuller transcript of his Monetary Matters appearance or additional appearances not currently captured in the corpus.

person/max-wiethe.text:
Max Wiethe is a financial media host, producer, and markets commentator whose profile in this corpus rests almost entirely on his work behind the microphone rather than on any documented market calls. He is best known for his time at Real Vision, where he hosted and produced programs including The Daily Briefing and trade-focused segments, and he has built a reputation as an interviewer who draws out traders, investors, and strategists while making markets accessible to retail audiences. His appearance here comes as an interview guest on The Monetary Matters Network.

Beyond that, the record is thin — and it should be said plainly. The digest contains no cited quotes, no dated stances, and no bullish, bearish, or neutral positions attributed to Wiethe, so there is no timeline of his views to trace and no strongest calls to name. As of now, he registers in this corpus as a media figure and convener of market debate rather than a participant with a trackable portfolio of positions; any portrait of his own investment views would require sources this record does not yet contain.

person/mike-alfred.text:
Mike Alfred is an American fintech entrepreneur who has spent his career turning financial data into businesses, and who has since recast himself as a professional Bitcoin investor and mining-sector commentator. With his brother Ryan he co-founded BrightScope, the retirement-plan ratings company acquired in 2016, and later co-founded Digital Assets Data, a crypto market-intelligence firm whose platform was bought by Coinbase — after which Alfred took a market intelligence role inside the exchange. Today he is best known in markets circles as a relentless presence on X covering Bitcoin and the publicly traded miners, and as a board member of Bitcoin miner Iris Energy (IREN), the company at the heart of his public investing identity. He is a self-described long-term Bitcoin holder, and nearly everything in this record comes from a single June 2026 appearance on Real Vision, an episode pointedly titled "The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)).

The thesis he laid out there is coherent and blunt. AI has been the only game in town — "the only thing that that has benefited over the last 3 years in mass is AI," with the S&P 500 carried by its largest, most-exposed companies — and the binding constraint on the trade is not chips but electricity: whether you "can spin up heavy-duty infrastructure… that you can keep online and you can run it at low price" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). That is the "hidden" leg of his argument: land, power and compute, with Bitcoin miners that already control cheap power positioned to pivot into AI workloads. His conviction is explicitly long-horizon — "over 5, 10, 15 years, I think there's still quite a bit of opportunity here because the market largely still doesn't understand these economic mo[ats]" — and he thinks it would be "a mistake in my opinion" to get too cautious about the theme "unless you really have to manage for like very short-term drawdowns and short-term performance" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)).

On his own positioning, Alfred is unusually tidy. Bitcoin is "really the only position that I've sort of publicly espoused over that period," he says, describing it as a straight long holding ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). On IREN the record is formally tagged "neutral," but that label does a lot of diplomatic work: as a director he says "I'm on the board, so I can't… give you advice to buy it," while volunteering that he's "never sold a share of Iron, even though it's gone from 28 to 1 to 75 to 28 to to 60," that "it's unlikely I'd be selling anything," and that his personal bet is "if Iron could pull this off at scale, it'll be very hard to compete with them" — the transcript's "Iron" being IREN itself ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). The neutrality, in other words, is a governance constraint, not a hesitation.

A caveat about the record itself: this corpus contains one appearance, on one day — twelve bullish stances, two neutral, zero bearish, all from the same interview. There is no timeline to trace, no pivot from skeptic to believer or back; what we can say is that as of June 2026 Alfred arrived with a fully formed power-and-compute thesis and a documented habit of holding IREN through a violent round trip. His consistency is asserted rather than observed here, and anyone citing his track record from this material is really citing one confident hour of television.

person/patrick-boyle.text:
Patrick Boyle is an Irish-born finance professional who has worn most of the hats the industry has to offer: derivatives trader at London investment banks, founder and manager of a volatility-focused hedge fund (the Palomar Fund), and lecturer in finance at King's College London and Queen Mary University of London. He has also written several books on quantitative finance, including *Trading and Pricing Financial Derivatives* and *Financial Derivatives: A Quantitative Finance View*. But his public profile rests mainly on his eponymous YouTube channel, where he delivers dry, frequently sardonic commentary on markets, economics, and business news — the persona of a practitioner who has seen the machinery up close and is unimpressed by the sales pitch.

The stance record captured here is unusually thin, and it should be read with that caveat: every position tagged to Boyle — four bearish, one bullish — comes from a single video, "How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon," published June 20, 2026. That said, the argument in it is a coherent and pointed one. Boyle's core bearish case is that American AI leadership is being squandered by its own export-control regime. "If AI is not a natural monopoly, and foreign competitors are offering models that are good enough, immune to US kill switches, and 60 times cheaper," the US edge evaporates ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)). His sharpest line lands on the market implications: "When your target market shrinks from the entire global economy to people who have passed a background check in Washington, your near trillion-dollar…" — the truncation is the digest's, but the direction is unmistakable ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)).

The flip side of that trade is his one bullish stance, on Chinese AI. Because models from Chinese firms like Jipu and DeepSeek are open-source and self-hostable — "companies can run on their own servers" — he sees them as the natural beneficiaries of foreign buyers who want capability without Washington's leverage ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)). Worth flagging for the reader: the bearish tags on broad market indices and on rates, bonds, and the dollar all trace back to the same Washington quote, so this is really one integrated argument about US AI dominance rather than four independent calls. There is no earlier positioning in the record to chart — no observable evolution from bull to bear or the reverse — so any claim about how Boyle's views have "moved over time" would be invention. What the record does show is a commentator whose instinct, at least on this occasion, runs against the consensus that AI is a durable American franchise.

person/patrick-ceresna.text:
Patrick Ceresna is a Canadian market strategist and technical analyst, Co-Founder and Chief Market Strategist of MacroVoices Media, and the voice of the weekly "MacroVoices Market Snapshot" segment on the MacroVoices podcast. His beat is chart-based technical analysis across equities, interest rates, currencies, and commodities, and what distinguishes him from most commentary hosts is that he attaches trades to the tape — derivatives and options structures, with bull call spreads a house specialty — rather than stopping at directional hand-waving. The credentials back the craft: he holds the Chartered Market Technician (CMT), Chartered Investment Manager (CIM), and Derivatives Market Specialist (DMS) designations, with roughly two decades in capital markets. His stance record in this corpus — 12 bullish calls against 7 bearish and 35 neutral — captures the disposition: a technician who waits for the chart to confirm before committing, and whose most frequent honest answer is "not yet."

The fullest window into his positioning comes from June 18–19, 2026, around MacroVoices #537 with Brent Johnson. On rates, Ceresna argued it is "very reasonable to assume that the yields near the 470 will be a key high," while yields sat under 4.5% but were "still not officially breaking into a new downtrend" — so no rush: it "doesn't make it an immediate opportunity to go long bonds" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ), [Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). On the dollar he was more decisive, seeing "clear US dollar strength here and flows coming into the US maybe chasing some of these equity returns" ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)) — a read that dovetailed neatly with his guest's no-turning-back dollar thesis — though even there he hedged, noting that the 160 level "has been a rock solid overhead resistance where we have seen numerous interventions happen in the past" ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). Gold drew his most disciplined non-call: "we have not yet actually seen a bullish pivot in the trend," he said, declining to rule out a retest of the lows even while insisting "there will be another gold bull market" — just one that lines up with conditions, not sentiment ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ), [MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)).

Energy is where he put real money behind a view. After the Iranian peace deal produced "dramatic repricing week over a week" with the most notable moves in crude ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)), Ceresna called for prices to "settle back above 80 at some point here and maybe even as high as 90," with the short term still unresolved ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). He argued "the bigger opportunity may come later through the knock-on effects on fertilizers, chemicals, and other crop support inputs" disrupted during the crisis ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)) — and that thesis became his Trade of the Week: with the agriculture ETF DBA at $26.84, buy the January 15, 2027 $27 strike call for $1.70 and sell the $30 strike call for $0.80, a 27-by-30 bull call spread for a $0.90 net debit with roughly 211 days to run ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ), [Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). Elsewhere he stayed in wait-and-see mode: uranium charts "remain relatively distributed" while he hunts for where those stocks will settle and when investors flow back in ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There's No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)), and he is watching whether "rebalancing and rotation out of the things that worked, which is energy stocks and some semiconductors," emerges now that the oil crisis has passed ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)).

A caveat the record demands: this corpus is thin on time depth. Every citation clusters inside a single 48-hour window on June 18–19, 2026 — three recordings of the same episode — so there is no genuine arc to trace yet. His current profile (bullish dollar, rates and crude; bearish the ten-year yield; deliberately neutral on gold, uranium, and semis) is one week's snapshot of a disciplined technician, not a documented evolution, and this page should be revisited as more Market Snapshot segments accumulate.

person/raoul-pal.text:
Raoul Pal is a British macro investor, financial media entrepreneur and writer whose career runs from the equities and equity-derivatives sales desks of Goldman Sachs — where he co-managed the European hedge fund sales business — to a global macro portfolio at GLG Partners, before he retired from fund management in his early thirties. He then rebuilt himself as a research and media entrepreneur: in 2005 he founded Global Macro Investor (GMI), an institutional macro research publication, and in 2014 he co-founded Real Vision, the subscription platform for long-form investor interviews, serving as its CEO. Today he writes and hosts The Journeyman, a newsletter, video and podcast series covering macro, markets and crypto, and he has become one of the most recognizable advocates of Bitcoin and crypto assets — a case he packages as his "Exponential Age" thesis.

The recorded calls in this corpus are unabashedly bullish, and the strongest of them come from a single June 18, 2026 episode of his show, "AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty," where he fuses the crypto and AI legs of his argument into one. On crypto, he argued that adoption by the financial system is "the thing that was required" for the asset class to become "the base of money" for the whole system ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)), and he pushed the idea further, envisioning "a world of super abundance" in which "Bitcoin becomes actually very important in a massively deflationary world" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). On AI and semiconductors, his bullishness takes an unusual form: he sees "an inability for a lot of this infrastructure to go bust, which is a really interesting thing that we've not seen before" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)) — a capex boom that, in his telling, comes with a built-in floor.

That is both the strength and the limit of the record here. Every stance captured is bullish — three for three, with no bearish or neutral calls logged — and all of it dates to that one episode, so the timeline reads as a snapshot rather than an evolution; whether Pal has hedged, reversed or doubled down elsewhere cannot be determined from this material. What the snapshot does show is the distinctive shape of his argument: Bitcoin as the monetary anchor of an AI-driven deflationary boom, a synthesis he presses far more explicitly than most macro commentators bother to attempt.

person/raoul-pal-palvatar-ai-avatar.text:
Raoul Pal is a British former hedge fund manager turned macro commentator, and in the past decade one of the most recognizable faces in financial media. He cut his teeth at Goldman Sachs, co-managing the hedge fund sales business in European equities and equity derivatives, then co-managed the GLG Global Macro Fund before retiring from fund management in his mid-30s. Rather than disappearing, he built a second act as a publisher: he founded Global Macro Investor (GMI), a subscription macro research service, and in 2014 co-founded Real Vision, the financial media and education company where he serves as CEO. He hosts the podcast "The Journeyman," is widely known on social media as @RaoulGMI, works largely out of the Cayman Islands, and has spoken openly about his multiple sclerosis diagnosis.

Intellectually, Pal is best understood as a big-picture pessimist about the existing system who converted that pessimism into an aggressive bull case for crypto. His core material is debt cycles, demographics, and what he calls the "Exponential Age" and the "Everything Code" — theses he has popularized arguing that technology-driven compounding is reshaping economies faster than legacy institutions can adapt. That framework made him one of the loudest institutional-finance voices championing Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the broader crypto asset class, a position that defines much of his public profile. "Palvatar," for the record, is an AI-generated avatar of Pal used in Real Vision and related content — a fitting accessory for a man whose brand is built on the exponential thesis.

On the evidentiary record in this corpus, however, Pal's footprint is thin: he appears as a guest on his own show ("Raoul Pal The Journeyman") with a single documented appearance, no tagged bullish, bearish, or neutral stances, and no dated topic timelines. That means the digest offers nothing yet on how his calls may have shifted over time, and no specific market positions can be cited with confidence from this material. Readers should treat the portrait above as biographical context; the dated, citation-backed calls — the substance of a market track record — remain to be captured.

person/shawn-hackett.text:
Shawn Hackett is an agricultural commodities strategist — president of Hackett Financial Advisors and a weather-cycle specialist of the look-at-the-dust-clouds-before-the-balance-sheet school — and in this corpus he appears exactly once, on Real Vision on June 14, 2026, in an episode pointedly titled "Why This El Niño Could Be Different." His pitch that day was that the looming El Niño carries "the implications for many so critical food supply items globally" and, beyond prices, "what it even might mean for governments and geopolitics" — food inflation framed as a macro and geopolitical force rather than a farm-gate curiosity ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)).

His strongest call is a historical analog: in a comparable prior episode, he argued, "the average price for rice and wheat" rose "600% during that period of time" — a number deployed to suggest the move in grains and softs could be violent rather than gradual ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)). Layered on top is a more idiosyncratic signal: "some of the highest concentrations of Arabian Peninsula sand in the atmosphere that we've seen since 2002," a dust-load reading his framework treats as a tell for what comes next. The record tags that dust observation as the lone bearish item in an otherwise bullish package — three bullish calls to one bearish, all from the same sitting, which says more about how he stacks evidence than about any hedging of the thesis ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)).

The honest caveat is that this page currently rests on a single June 2026 conversation, so there is no timeline to trace — no earlier bearish turn or later capitulation, just one concentrated blast of El Niño-for-food-supply urgency. A "bullish China & Hong Kong equities" tag also shows up in the record, but it hangs off the same food-supply-and-geopolitics quote rather than any direct equity call, so treat it as thin until he shows up again ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)). Whether rice and wheat did anything resembling a 600% run after his appearance, the digest doesn't say — and neither will we.

person/steve.text:
Steve Van Metre is a U.S.-based investment adviser and bond-market commentator whose YouTube channel is devoted to the Treasury market, the dollar system, and Federal Reserve policy. He sits squarely in the "eurodollar" school popularized by Jeff Snider — the view that global dollar liquidity, not Fed policy alone, drives markets — and he is a recurring guest on Eurodollar University and on podcasts hosted by Snider and Emil Kalinowski, where he works through yield curves, debt issuance, and money markets. He is best known for a long-running bullish Treasury thesis, the widely followed "TLT trade" (long call options on the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF), premised on falling long-term yields as recession and dollar-shortage dynamics unfold.

The record in this corpus captures him mid-thesis, across two Eurodollar University appearances a week apart in June 2026. On June 14, in the wake of the Iran conflict, he argued the real oil crisis was only beginning: the "big shoe to drop over the next couple of months" is a supply problem, with "India... without sufficient diesel for several weeks if not months further on" ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). Yet his headline price call is deflationary, not inflationary — oil at $50 a barrel, but "not because there's just a sudden flood of supply in the market. It's the demand destruction, the coming rec[ession]" — paired with a warning that "inflation is going to just come right down isn't so likely at least in the short-term" ([Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)). The shape of the call is a near-term squeeze giving way to a demand-driven collapse, which is the recession thesis his bond trade depends on.

A week later he sharpened the macro side. Reacting to the Swiss bond market, he insisted "the shock is growing, it's real" even though "spending's up, market's up," and he was categorical on policy: "are rates going to continue to drop and go negative? Absolutely. Will central bankers panic? Absolutely. Is it going to work? I don't think it's goin[g to]" ([Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4)). Falling yields plus impotent central banks is exactly the environment the TLT trade is built for.

On movement over time, the honest answer is that this record can't show it: two shows in one week, uniformly bearish (nine bearish stances against two bullish tags, one of which — a China-equities flag resting on an oil-supply quote — reads more like a coding artifact than a genuine call). What it does show is consistency: a dollar-shortage recession thesis applied across oil, rates, and the broad economy, with no hedging in sight.

person/steve-van-metre.text:
Steve Van Metre is an American financial advisor and portfolio manager who runs Van Metre & Co. — also known as Steve Van Metre Financial Services — a wealth-management and registered investment advisory firm based in Bakersfield, California. His public profile, however, extends well beyond the RIA business: he maintains a popular YouTube channel and podcast presence centered on global macroeconomics, and he is a frequent guest on the macro and finance podcast circuit, where he has built a following as one of the most consistently dollar-bullish voices in the space.

The core of his argument is a structural shortage of U.S. dollars, grounded in Eurodollar-system analysis — the view that offshore dollar credit creation, not Fed policy, drives global liquidity, and that this system has been contracting. From that premise he extrapolates a deflationary bust in risk assets and credit, and his standing counsel to clients and viewers is to hold dollars and short-duration Treasuries ahead of a liquidity-driven crisis. It is a框架 that cuts hard against the inflation-and-debasement consensus that dominates mainstream macro commentary, and that contrarian positioning — long the world's "safe" liability rather than its hard assets — is essentially his brand.

The record in this corpus is thin, and it should be said plainly: Van Metre appears exactly once, as a guest on Eurodollar University, with no bullish, bearish, or neutral stances logged and no dated topic timelines attached. That means his strongest calls cannot be pinned to specific dates here, and no evolution of his views — sharpening, hedging, or reversal — can be charted from what has been captured. What the record does establish is the durable shape of the position: a deflationist holding pattern, waiting on a dollar-shortage event that the corpus has not yet tracked him either calling correctly or abandoning.

person/tony.text:
Tony's presence in this corpus rests on a single appearance: a guest spot on The Macro Dirt Podcast on June 23, 2026, in an episode headlined around George Noble's takes on stocks, gold, oil and AI ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). On that show he made one clear, dated call — he was buying crude oil at prevailing levels: "I'm a buyer down here of oil as well" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). The stance registers on both the crude futures (CL=F) timeline and the broader Oil & Energy theme, though it is the same quote doing double duty rather than two separate calls.

The "as well" in his phrasing suggests he was piling onto a bullish oil case already on the table that day, not carving out a contrarian position. Beyond that, the record is thin and should be read as such: one appearance, one direction, no bearish or neutral stances logged, and no follow-up interviews that would show whether he held, added to, or ditched the oil buy. There is no arc to trace yet. As of late June 2026, Tony's profile is a snapshot — an oil dip-buyer, full stop — and any portrait of how his views move over time will have to wait on further appearances.

person/tony-greer.text:
Tony Greer is a financial markets analyst and newsletter author best known for The Morning Navigator, a daily macro commentary that tracks momentum, liquidity, and price action across equities, currencies, commodities, and crypto. His pedigree is sell-side trading rather than academia: he spent roughly a decade at Goldman Sachs in the firm's currency and commodities businesses before striking out as an independent researcher. That background shows in how he talks about markets — less narrative, more tape. Greer's approach is fundamentally flows- and momentum-driven; he cares about where liquidity is going and what price action confirms, and he has built his public profile largely through financial media and podcast appearances on CNBC, Real Vision, and a circuit of macro-focused shows.

What Greer argues for, at his core, is discipline over conviction: follow the momentum, respect the liquidity backdrop, and let price action arbitrate between bullish and bearish stories. It is a trader's framework rather than a permabull or permabear ideology, which is part of why he circulates widely across media with very different audiences — his lens travels well because it is not anchored to a single asset-class allegiance.

The record captured here, however, is thin on specifics. Greer appears twice as a guest on The Macro Dirt Podcast, but the digest contains no extracted stances, dated calls, or topic timelines — no documented bullish or bearish positions, and therefore no visible evolution in his views over time. For a wiki page intending to track his strongest calls with dates and citations, the sourcing simply is not there yet; anyone relying on this corpus alone would have his framework and biography, but not his market record.

person/tony-greer-and-jared-dillian.text:
Tony Greer and Jared Dillian are a pairing of two trading-desk veterans turned macro commentators — Greer of the TG Macro morning note, with a background as a gold trader at Goldman Sachs, and Dillian of The Daily Dirtnap, formerly head of ETF trading at Lehman Brothers. In this corpus, though, their joint footprint rests on a single appearance: the June 17, 2026 discussion "[Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)," which sweeps across rates, currencies, energy, metals and even private-space assets in one sitting.

The through-line of that conversation is a coherent disinflationary, liquidity-friendly macro view. The headline call is that "bonds may be the world's most underowned asset" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)), paired explicitly with "dollar weakness" and a bearish read on energy amid "collapsing oil prices" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). That long-bonds, short-dollar, weak-oil configuration is classic disinflation trading — and it makes their hesitation on gold the notable exception. Rather than riding the metals rally, they sit neutral, weighing "what gold's recent correction signals for the precious metals sector" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). Meanwhile the speculative appetite they decline to spend on gold shows up elsewhere: they ask "whether SpaceX is becoming the ultimate momentum trade as capital rotates across global markets" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)), a tell that they see froth rotating into private-side stories even as they position for lower rates.

The honest caveat: this is a one-day snapshot. Every stance on record dates to June 17, 2026 and a single source, so there is no timeline yet to show whether the bond-bullishness is a fresh turn or a long-held conviction, or how they've handled the gold correction before or since. Treat this as a snapshot of where the two stood on one afternoon, not a track record.

person/val-zlatev.text:
Val Zlatev is a portfolio manager at Diamond Hill Capital Management, the Columbus, Ohio-based asset manager, where he joined as a research analyst in the early 2010s and now co-manages the firm's large-cap equity strategies. His beat is technology and semiconductors — he has discussed memory-chip makers Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix in financial media and on investing podcasts — and his style of argument is bottoms-up and specific: head counts, supply chains, and deal math rather than narrative.

His strongest documented call comes from a single appearance on June 20, 2026, on The Monetary Matters Network, sharing an episode pointedly titled "Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits" with veteran short-seller Jim Chanos. Against the bear case that AI profits are an accounting mirage, Zlatev offered a labor-based rebuttal: "look at head counts over the last three or four years compared to the operating profits of these companies," where the divergence between flat staffing and surging profits is, in his telling, evidence of real productivity rather than financial engineering ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). His structural bull case concentrated in memory, arguing that high-demand memory names trade at "cheap forward multiples" because the physical supply chain constrains how quickly capacity can arrive ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). The framing is unambiguous about where value sits in the AI stack: "Technology is the ultimate differentiator in that game... the value add is in the chips and the wrappers of the chips" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

What makes the appearance worth studying is that the bullishness is selectively applied rather than wholesale. He conceded that where AI infrastructure deals actually disclose their economics, they are "penciling out at 7%, 6%, 5%, 8%" — thin returns that cut against the buildout's math — and he flagged outright "shorting opportunities on a bunch of component makers" selling into PCs and smartphones, the devices being displaced by the data-center boom ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). On the three big memory producers — "one of which is American, two of which are Korean" — he acknowledged the stocks "have gone up so much" even while pressing the structural case ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). He kept two hedges in view: that demand can be tracked in real time through open-routed token counts and GPU rental prices, and that a genuinely new, non-transformer model architecture could scramble the chip stack ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). His meta-take on the debate itself is notably balanced — "there's probably just as many bears as bulls on the AI argument, which I think is extremely healthy" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

The honest caveat: this is a one-interview record. All thirteen logged stances — six bullish, three bearish, four neutral — carry the same June 2026 timestamp, so there is no arc to trace, no earlier positioning to compare against, no reversals to chronicle. The archive also tags him bearish on precious metals, but the supporting quote is the same 5–8% AI-deal-return passage, not anything about gold or silver; that tag looks like a filing artifact and should not be read as a metals call. What the snapshot does establish is a coherent identity: a memory-and-silicon bull who thinks the bears perform a useful function, checks the hype against token counts and deal math, and is willing to short the casualties inside his own theme.

person/aminvest.text:
aminvest is a solo author writing a self-titled, Traditional Chinese-language investing newsletter (Hong Kong/Cantonese in flavour) that covers U.S. equities for a Patreon audience. The eleven posts captured here skew hard toward the hyped end of the market — SpaceX-linked SPCX, semiconductor names like Micron, and mega-cap financials such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — and the house style is analytical with a contrarian streak: the recurring move is telling readers that a dip in a crowd favourite is not automatically a bargain. The stance mix across the corpus (8 bullish, 6 bearish, 6 neutral) suggests balance, but the sequencing tells a sharper story.

The arc over the captured window — a mere ten days in June 2026 — begins constructively. On June 15, aminvest was widening the net beyond tech, saying they would "start watching investment-bank stocks whose momentum is strengthening" ([美股市況短評 (20260615)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161146651)); two days later they liked Goldman Sachs but called the stock "on the high side" and hard to buy ([美股市況短評 (20260617)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161328901)). On June 18 the stance was still bullish, arguing that large-cap tech with strong cash flows, if it corrected and stabilised, "could actually be a buying opportunity" ([美股市況短評 (20260618)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161407746)). Even the neutrality on the broad market read as genuine two-way uncertainty — U.S. indices at "a key resistance level: attack, or defend?" with the day's trade "critical" ([美股市況短評 (20260622)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161763918)).

Then came the pivot, and it ran through credit. On June 23 aminvest flagged that "the corporate credit market has already started to deteriorate" and warned that Hong Kong stocks "may already have entered phase two of a bear market" ([美股市況短評 (20260623)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161861803)); by June 25 the language hardened to "corporate debt default ratios have already begun to deteriorate," which the corpus logs as a formal bullish-to-bearish flip on rates, bonds and the dollar in a single week ([美股市況短評 (20260625)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-162048909)). The strongest single call, though, is on SPCX: on June 24, aminvest dismissed the bargain-hunters bluntly — if you think SPCX below $150 is already cheap, "that thinking is a bit naive" — and punctuated it by asking an AI model at what SPCX price Elon Musk would lose his richest-man status, getting $17.61 back ([美股市況短評 (20260624)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161958989)).

The most interesting tension sits inside the June 25 post itself, which is logged as both bullish and bearish on AI and semiconductors: aminvest simultaneously said many large-cap tech stocks "should rise further" and that "many AI-related and unrelated companies around the world will go bankrupt" ([美股市況短評 (20260625)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-162048909)). Read together, that is less a contradiction than a narrow-leadership argument — the mega-caps keep climbing while the long tail of the AI complex fails — but the corpus doesn't spell that out, so treat it as interpretation. The honest caveat: this is thin coverage, eleven posts across June 15–25, 2026, and the "evolution" is really one fast, credit-driven turn inside a fortnight. Whether the bearish credit call held is not something the digest can show.

person/person-001.text:
何啟聰 (Ho Kai-chung) is a Hong Kong markets man of the derivatives desk rather than the research floor: a long-time UBS banker who rose to Managing Director and head of ETF and OTC derivatives sales for the bank's Hong Kong business, and who has become one of the city's most recognisable commentators on leveraged and inverse products, warrants and bull/bear certificates. He fronts his own bylined column for the Hong Kong Economic Journal, and his natural beat is the plumbing of retail trading — ETF flows, structured products, and whatever sector is driving Hong Kong turnover at the moment.

The captured record is narrow — three columns across a single week in June 2026 — but the tilt is unmistakable: of nineteen tagged stances, twelve are bearish, six neutral, just one bullish. His hardest call came on 19 June 2026, arguing that AI hardware price inflation has backed the Fed into a corner, noting that Fed Chair Warsh used his first meeting to warn that US inflation sits far above the 2% target with energy only one of the pressures. The read-through to Hong Kong was blunt: Alibaba (9988.HK) and Tencent (0700.HK) are falling, in his telling, because persistently dearer AI hardware will keep inflating cloud capex, while the AI price war is already asymmetric — Tencent and Alibaba raising prices only for JD.com (9618.HK) to respond with cuts, and large-model token prices racing to the bottom ([AI硬件漲價逼聯儲局入死角](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4435475/AI%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E6%BC%B2%E5%83%B9%E9%80%BC%E8%81%AF%E5%84%B2%E5%B1%80%E5%85%A5%E6%AD%BB%E8%A7%92)).

Two further columns sharpen the picture. On 22 June he skewered the valuation disconnect between private-market euphoria and unloved Hong Kong earnings — SpaceX chased despite no profits while profitable HK stocks get dumped — and used SMIC (0981.HK) as his cautionary tale, recalling that when the chipmaker listed A-shares in 2020 the H-shares fell on day one and holders needed five years to get back to breakeven ([SpaceX溢價僅馬斯克獨有](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4436065/SpaceX%E6%BA%A2%E5%83%B9%E5%83%85%E9%A6%AC%E6%96%AF%E5%85%8B%E7%8D%A8%E6%9C%89)). On 26 June he was on home turf with his signature theme: leveraged-ETF concentration risk. He warned that as Hynix-linked leveraged ETFs balloon in size, a sharp fall in the stock could pose systemic risk to Korean markets, citing the episode where mere tax-talk knocked Hynix and dragged the KOSPI 200 down a tenth with leveraged products amplifying the move, and he expects Korean regulators to act if the swelling continues ([海力士槓桿ETF威脅韓股](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440216/%E6%B5%B7%E5%8A%9B%E5%A3%AB%E6%A7%93%E6%A1%BFETF%E5%A8%81%E8%84%85%E9%9F%93%E8%82%A1)). The kicker is that Hong Kong is running the same experiment: he flagged local investors piling into the two-times leveraged ETF (07709), whose net assets had already hit HK$130 billion — larger than the Tracker Fund (02800) itself.

Within the week, the drift ran one way: his China and Hong Kong equities stance sat neutral on 19 and 22 June before turning bearish on 26 June, alongside a macro call that was bearish from the start. But eight days is a snapshot, not a trajectory — the corpus contains no earlier columns to test whether this defensiveness is a settled stance or a mood, and the lone bullish tick in the tally is not tied to any dated call in the record. Read him, for now, as a structured-products specialist warning a leverage-saturated market that its exits are narrower than they look.

person/paul-krugman.text:
克魯明（Paul Krugman）是美國經濟學家及專欄作家，2008 年獲諾貝爾經濟學獎，表揚他對貿易模式與經濟活動區位的分析。他先後執教於麻省理工、普林斯頓，2015 年起轉往紐約市立大學研究生中心；2000 年起在《紐約時報》撰寫「The Conscience of a Liberal」專欄，直至 2024 年底退休，長期是宏觀政策辯論中最具分貝、也最鮮明站在民主黨一側的凱恩斯主義聲音。面向一般讀者的著作包括《The Return of Depression Economics》、《End This Depression Now!》及《Arguing with Zombies》。

他的立場輪廓清楚：主張積極財政與寬鬆貨幣政策對抗衰退、反對緊縮，關注貿易、不平等與政治經濟學的交叉地帶。爭議性亦同樣出名——行文辛辣、黨派色彩濃厚，讚賞者視之為敢言，批評者則認為他把分析讓位於政治。

在本資料庫的覆蓋而言，克魯明的紀錄相當單薄：他僅以訪談嘉賓身份出現一次，節目為徐家健主持；未有記錄任何看好、看淡或中性的具體立場，亦沒有可追蹤的主題時間線，因此無法從本庫引述他帶日期的具體判斷或觀點轉變。以上 portrait 中的年期能提供背景，但他的市場與政策呼籚，需待更多收錄方可印證。

person/person-002.text:
劉強東 (Liu Qiangdong, widely known as Richard Liu) is the founder and chairman of JD.com and the archetype of the self-built Chinese e-commerce empire. Born to a poor rural family in Suqian, Jiangsu, he graduated from Renmin University in 1996, burned through a failed restaurant venture, and in 1998 opened a small electronics stall in Beijing's Zhongguancun technology district that grew into Jingdong. The 2003 SARS epidemic pushed him to pivot the business online, and his answer to a market awash in counterfeits was brute-force vertical integration — self-built warehousing and a self-run delivery network to guarantee authentic goods and fast service. That bet scaled into a NASDAQ listing in May 2014, one of the largest Chinese tech IPOs of its time, a secondary listing in Hong Kong in 2020, and an ecosystem spanning JD Logistics, JD Health, and JD Technology (formerly JD Digits). Liu stepped down as CEO in April 2022 but retained the chairmanship and controlling influence over the company. He remains one of China's wealthiest individuals, is married to Zhang Zetian, and is known both for philanthropy in his hometown and for a paternalistic management style toward JD's army of couriers. The record is not unblemished: a 2018 sexual-assault allegation in Minnesota dented his reputation, though it resulted in no charges and ended in a settled civil suit.

For an investment corpus, the stance file on Liu is thin to the point of being a single data point: one bearish call on China & Hong Kong equities, with nothing bullish or neutral recorded against it. Dated 23 June 2026, the tag rests on one remark — 「將來都是機械人送貨了，根本不需要快遞員。」("In the future it will all be robots delivering; couriers simply won't be needed") — made in the context of a report on JD couriers facing retraining ([京東不要快遞員 三項鐵人再培訓](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4436952/%E4%BA%AC%E6%9D%B1%E4%B8%8D%E8%A6%81%E5%BF%AB%E9%81%9E%E5%93%A1+%E4%B8%89%E9%A0%85%E9%90%B5%E4%BA%BA%E5%86%8D%E5%9F%B9%E8%A8%93)).

Whether that adds up to a genuine bearish view on Chinese stocks, or simply a founder talking about automating his own workforce, is an open question — and the remark sits in obvious tension with his long-cultivated image as the boss who treats couriers like family. With no earlier positioning in the timeline to compare against, there is no arc of a view "moving over time" to report here; the single bearish tag should be treated as provisional, reflecting automation risk inside JD's own delivery network as much as any macro call on the market.

person/person-003.text:
Shih Wing-ching (施永青) occupies a rare position in Hong Kong's property debate: he is both its most credentialed insider and one of its most quotable outside voices. Born in Shanghai in 1949, he co-founded Centaline Property Agency (中原地產) in 1978 and built it into one of the largest real-estate agencies in Hong Kong and mainland China, then founded the free Chinese-language newspaper am730 in 2005 as a platform for his widely read columns on property, economics and current affairs. His free-market, Daoist-inflected commentary has made "施老闆" — Boss Shih — one of the city's most quoted voices on housing, precisely because he speaks with an operator's knowledge and a philosopher's shrug.

The corpus on him here is thin — a single entry, captured in Kao Tin-yau's (高天佑) Hong Kong Economic Journal column of June 17, 2026, titled 北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青 — roughly, "mainland money's speculative fervor rattles Shih Wing-ching" ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)). But that one snapshot catches him doing what he does best: holding a bullish call and a bearish warning in the same breath. On the bullish side, the column records him standing alone against consensus, projecting gains of as much as 15% — "施老闆已獨排眾議，揚言升幅可達15%" ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)). Yet the same frenzy apparently unnerved him, because his deeper objection is to froth rather than to appreciation: speculators, he argues, "會把樓價推至一個用家負擔不起的水平，繼而妨礙民生" — push home prices beyond what end-users can afford, and in doing so damage livelihoods ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)). His ideal sits between the two: prices rising "穩定地緩緩地隨經濟增長一起同步上升" — steadily, slowly, in step with economic growth ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)).

The data structure itself deserves a caveat. The taggers score him two bullish, two bearish and two neutral stances — but all six come from this single article, split across his China & Hong Kong equities and China property timelines, both of which are marked "now bearish" ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)). With only one dated item, there is no way to chart how his views have moved over time; the "movement" here is intra-column, not inter-temporal. Read carefully, though, the posture is coherent rather than contradictory: Shih is bullish on legitimate upside, hostile to hot-money distortion, and anchored to a fundamentals-aligned, steady-rise view of what property markets should do — a stance of tolerance for gains and intolerance for the gamblers who spoil them.

person/person-004.text:
李聲揚 is a Hong Kong–based finance writer and commentator who has built his career translating the value-investing canon — Benjamin Graham's margin-of-safety logic, Warren Buffett's owner-oriented stock-picking — for a Chinese-speaking audience. He does this across formats: columns for Hong Kong financial media, Chinese-language books on stock-picking and value investing, and a steady stream of speaking and podcast commentary on Hong Kong equities and personal investing. The pitch, at root, is that bottom-up analysis of individual businesses matters more than anything happening in the macro swirl around them.

That conviction shows up clearly in the one dated item this record captures. In a June 26, 2026 column for Hong Kong's HKEJ, pointedly titled 宏觀交易過五關 AI落場都輸錢 ("macro trading passes five gates; even AI loses money on the field"), 李聲揚 took aim at the entire enterprise of macro-based investing: "事實上，即使能未卜先知，了解局勢走向，對投資近乎是零幫助，甚至是催命符" — even perfect foresight of how events will unfold is near-zero help to investors, and may in fact be a death sentence ([宏觀交易過五關 AI落場都輸錢](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440220/%E5%AE%8F%E8%A7%80%E4%BA%A4%E6%98%93%E9%81%8E%E4%BA%94%E9%97%9C+AI%E8%90%BD%E5%A0%B4%E9%83%BD%E8%BC%B8%E9%8C%A2)). The piece is tagged neutral on broad market and macro indices, which fits: this is not a bullish or bearish call on markets but an argument that macro forecasting is worse than useless as an investment input — with a headline that extends the skepticism even to AI-driven macro traders.

Honesty compels a caveat about the evidence base: the corpus behind this page holds exactly one dated stance from him — zero bullish calls, zero bearish calls — so there is no real timeline of his views to trace yet. What it does establish is a temperament consistent with his value-investing brand: impatient with prediction, dismissive of edge claims in macro, and comfortable arguing that knowing the future wouldn't save you anyway. Whether his column record shows the same discipline on individual stock calls is a question this archive, at present, cannot answer.

person/person-005.text:
梁天卓 is a Hong Kong economist and financial columnist, best known as one-third of the「經濟3.0」(Economics 3.0) column in the Hong Kong Economic Journal (信報)， where he writes alongside 徐家健 and 曾國平 on applied economics, public policy, law and economics, and Hong Kong current affairs. He holds a doctorate in economics and has worked in Hong Kong's financial sector, and he also appears as a commentator and presenter in Cantonese economics media and podcasts. The profile that emerges is less market-timer than policy debater — an economist who takes whatever Hong Kong is arguing about and runs it through the machinery of incentives and institutional design.

That is exactly the register of the strongest call captured in this corpus. In a June 25, 2026 column, he took a position on legalizing autonomous driving, arguing that the more reasonable course is a “middle path”: a limited pilot scheme that approves only vetted systems, runs them in designated areas or on designated routes, obliges operators to submit data on mileage, takeovers, accidents, near misses and complaints, and then expands or narrows the programme's scope periodically according to what the data show ([自駕合法化 有限度先導計劃可取](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4439041/%E8%87%AA%E9%A7%95%E5%90%88%E6%B3%95%E5%8C%96+%E6%9C%89%E9%99%90%E5%BA%A6%E5%85%88%E5%B0%8E%E8%A8%88%E5%8A%83%E5%8F%AF%E5%8F%96)). The piece is logged as bullish twice — once under robotics, automation and autonomy, and once under China and Hong Kong equities — but both tags trace back to this single article, so the optimism on record is really an evidence-gated, gradualist stance toward the technology rather than a conventional equity call.

An honest caveat: the coverage here is thin. One dated article, two bullish tags derived from it, and no bearish or neutral positions on record — far too little to chart how his views have moved over time. What the snapshot does establish is method rather than market conviction: demand the data, start small, scale by results. That is classic Economics 3.0 DNA, and it is the through-line readers should expect from him on everything from transport policy onward — though whether he translates that analytical bent into actual directional market calls is something this record simply does not yet show.

person/person-006.text:
狂徒 is a pseudonymous Chinese-language investment commentator, best known as the creator and solo host of the show 狂徒投資 (Kuang Tu Investment), where he discusses stock markets and investing for a primarily Chinese-speaking audience. His real identity and personal background are not widely publicized, which is not unusual in this corner of the commentary world — the persona and the show are the product, and the analysis is delivered under the 狂徒 name rather than a verifiable professional track record.

Beyond that framing, the corpus is thin, and it is worth saying so plainly: the extracted record for 狂徒 contains no dated calls, no identifiable bullish, bearish, or neutral positions, and no topic timelines that would let us trace how his views have moved over time. As it stands, this portrait can establish who he is and what platform he argues from, but it cannot yet name his strongest calls or characterize the shape of his market views. Readers should treat this page as a stub pending the addition of cited episodes and positions from 狂徒投資.

person/person-007.text:
陳坤耀（Edward K. Y. Chen）是香港資深經濟學者及教育行政人員，1995至2007年出任嶺南大學校長，帶領該校轉型為完整的博雅大學；此前長期在香港大學任經濟學教授，曾任院長等高級職務，並與港大亞洲研究中心關係密切。他的研究與評論聚焦香港經濟、亞太新興工業化經濟體、技術轉移與發展經濟學，歷任多項政府諮詢及公職（包括消費者委員會主席），是香港媒體上活躍的經濟評論人和專欄作者。

在本語料庫中，陳坤耀以訪問嘉賓身份在「高天佑」出現一次，立場紀錄亦僅此一條，且被歸類為淡友：2026年6月16日，他談及香港科研基礎時直言「與新加坡、南韓、台灣等地方比較，我們的R&D（研究開發）投放很少，基礎比較薄弱。這幾年政府在追趕，但是R&D仍僅佔GDP 1.1%至1.2%，還需要加一把勁」，並提出北部都會區可借鑑「合肥模式」的政府主導投資思路（[北都可借鑑「合肥模式」](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4431990/%E5%8C%97%E9%83%BD%E5%8F%AF%E5%80%9F%E9%91%91%E3%80%8C%E5%90%88%E8%82%A5%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F%E3%80%8D)）。

必須說明：覆蓋極為單薄，僅憑一次發言無法勾勒其觀點的時間軌跡或立場轉變。而所謂「淡友」標籤，實質上更多指向他對香港創科投入長期落後於區內對手的結構性憂慮，而非對股市點位的明確判斷——這層細分，讀者引用時宜自行拿捏。

person/person-008.text:
高天佑 is a Hong Kong financial journalist and columnist in the classic 信報 mould: he writes the 新聞點評 column for the Hong Kong Economic Journal, cut his teeth in Apple Daily's finance pages, and voices audio and podcast versions of his own copy. In this corpus he is almost entirely a solo act — solo author or host on eight of ten appearances, a guest just twice — which suits the trade: one voice, a daily deadline, and a stance on whatever the market and the news cycle served up.

That stance, in the sampled record, is overwhelmingly bearish — 15 bearish calls against 4 bullish and 3 neutral — and the bear case is a coherent three-front story about the mainland washing over Hong Kong. On June 18, 2026 he argued that with mainland e-commerce "attacking" Hong Kong during the 618 shopping festival, local retailers — especially small and mid-sized physical merchants — "恐將更加難捱", unable to compete with 財雄勢大的內地巨擘, with the rot spreading to unemployment, shop vacancy, rents and property valuations ([618攻港 本地零售難捱](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4434076/618%E6%94%BB%E6%B8%AF+%E6%9C%AC%E5%9C%B0%E9%9B%B6%E5%94%AE%E9%9B%A3%E6%8D%B4)). Two days later he was on the mainland labour market: the economy slowing, employment "日益惡化", and anyone over 35 written off as a layoff high-risk group — filed, tellingly, under robotics and automation ([京東不要快遞員 三項鐵人再培訓](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4436952/%E4%BA%AC%E6%9D%B1%E4%B8%8D%E8%A6%81%E5%BF%AB%E9%81%9E%E5%93%A1+%E4%B8%89%E9%A0%85%E9%90%B5%E4%BA%BA%E5%86%8D%E5%9F%B9%E8%A8%93)). On June 24 he put a number on the property wreck: national home prices down more than 30% since the 2021 blowup ([《求是》響警號 內需新思維](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4437891/%E3%80%8A%E6%B1%82%E6%98%AF%E3%80%8B%E9%9F%BF%E8%AD%A6%E8%99%9F+%E5%85%A7%E9%9C%80%E6%96%B0%E6%80%9D%E7%B6%AD)).

What makes the portrait interesting is how fast the bull phase burned off. On June 16 he was genuinely upbeat on the China AI complex: Hefei's economy booming on the back of semiconductor firms "食正人工智能浪潮", with CXMT (長鑫科技) posting RMB 33 billion in first-quarter profit — "每日賺3.6億元" — as one of only four companies worldwide mass-producing HBM, and a lesson there for Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis ([北都可借鑑「合肥模式」](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4431990/%E5%8C%97%E9%83%BD%E5%8F%AF%E5%80%9F%E9%91%91%E3%80%8C%E5%90%88%E8%82%A5%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F%E3%80%8D)). Within 48 hours the same author had flipped bearish on both China/Hong Kong equities and broad macro, on the strength of the 618 retail carnage. The stance log then records a second bull-to-bear swing between June 24 and 25, right as global markets cracked — US AI leaders down more than 10% in a session, Korea's market off 9.99%, Hong Kong stocks at a one-year low — though that entry carries no linked article in the sample. He embraced the AI story and then turned on it almost the moment the tape broke.

Two honest caveats. The sampled window is barely ten days in June 2026, so the "flips" may say more about a daily columnist marking the news to market than about deep conviction change — his neutral entries are precisely where he lays out both sides, as in the June 17 piece framing the 防走資 debate as "兩種不同意見" ([北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92)), or his aside that Hong Kong consumers are short-term winners from e-commerce discounts ([618攻港 本地零售難捱](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4434076/618%E6%94%BB%E6%B8%AF+%E6%9C%AC%E5%9C%B0%E9%9B%B6%E5%94%AE%E9%9B%A3%E6%8D%B4)). The bearish tilt is real in the data; the churn is the job description. Coverage is thin — treat this as a snapshot, not a career arc.

So the timeline runs: a concrete bullish call in June tied to pricing news, then two months of silence punctuated by a shrug. The consensus label "bullish" rests on a single position, and the bear side of the ledger is simply empty rather than argued — anyone citing a genuine two-sided dispute on AAPL from this corpus would be overstating what's on the page.

ticker/BTC-USD.text:
The Bitcoin debate in this corpus is lopsided and, frankly, thin on conviction. The tally runs 1 bullish, 2 bearish, and 9 neutral, which sounds like genuine ambivalence until you look at who actually stuck their neck out: one loud long, two dismissive shorts-in-spirit, and a fat middle of commentators who mostly couldn't be bothered to pick a side. The itemized record spans barely two months, from late June to mid-August 2026, and the most articulate voice in it isn't even identified by name.

The bull case rests almost entirely on [Mike Alfred](../People/mike-alfred.md), who on June 21, 2026 described "a straight long Bitcoin position" as "really the only position that I've sort of publicly espoused over that period." That's the lone bullish call in the entire count, and notably it's a positioning statement rather than a thesis — no price target, no catalyst, just skin in the game.

The bears came out swinging two days later, and their argument is about relevance, not valuation. On June 23, the host Tony read the tape as "a story that is like coming to an end," while [George Noble](../People/george-noble.md) delivered the sharpest line of the cycle: "Bitcoin is the Facebook of speculative assets... I think it's just going to go into the sunset I just think it's irrelevant." The bear framing here is decay and displacement — an aging speculative vehicle fading rather than crashing on its own merits.

The most interesting evolution belongs to an unidentified commentator whose calls hardened visibly across the first half of August. On August 7, 2026 the stance was explicitly neutral — "I think we're kind of in this middle ground. I don't think it's an amazing like entry in either direction." Within a week the tone had turned: cryptocurrencies were "under a cloud because they're very liquidity sensitive" on August 11, and by August 13 the argument was that "crypto is under a cloud and gold has been outperforming, and that's really the story we think is likely to continue" — a relative-value bearishness that pairs the crypto call with a gold endorsement rather than a short thesis on Bitcoin itself. The same speaker sketched a conditional downside of a break below $40,000, though only in the event of a technical breakdown, so it reads as a risk scenario rather than a forecast.

Honest caveats: the digest is thin. Most of those nine neutral calls aren't itemized with named speakers, so the "consensus" is softer than the tally suggests, and the timeline is too short to show whether anyone reversed a real position rather than just a tone. The one clear mind-change is that August drift from middle ground to "under a cloud." Whether Alfred's lonely long gets vindicated or Noble's sunset scenario plays out is a question the record simply doesn't answer yet.

ticker/CAT.text:
The bull case on Caterpillar in this corpus rests almost entirely on one voice: Chris Semenuk, who laid out an unusually specific earnings path on June 18, 2026 — arguing the company is "capable of at least $10 a quarter by 2029," which would roughly mean earnings climbing from around $20 a share today ([Chris Semenuk](../People/chris-semenuk.md)). What makes his call more than a generic cyclical-recovery story is the angle he takes on it: he frames Caterpillar as a power-generation play, not just a yellow-iron maker — "I know you make large engines for construction equipment, but you also make power engines" — a nod to the demand pull from data center electrification that the market has mostly been awarding to other names ([Chris Semenuk](../People/chris-semenuk.md)). He also points to observable strength on the ground: construction industries growing across "all the yellow equipment," and a resource industries order backlog growing at a pace it hasn't seen in some time ([Chris Semenuk](../People/chris-semenuk.md)).

Semenuk's underlying thesis is quality-of-franchise: he groups Caterpillar with "Gates, Ingersoll Parker" as "extraordinarily well-managed businesses that have enormous cash flow" ([Chris Semenuk](../People/chris-semenuk.md)). That's a compounding-machine argument — the stock deserves to be valued on durable cash generation and a power-generation option most investors haven't fully priced.

To be plain about the limits of the record here: there is no real debate documented. The consensus tally stands at four bullish calls, zero bearish, and one neutral, but the digest only itemizes Semenuk's positions, and no speaker in this set has changed their mind on the name — no documented reversals, no counter-arguments, no named bear. The entire timeline of calls compresses into a single day, June 18, 2026. Readers should treat the bullish consensus as real but thinly sourced: one detailed advocate, on one date, with the skeptics — if they exist — simply absent from the record.
